lessons.title: Atomic Structure
lessons.objective: Distinguish atoms, molecules and ions, state the contributions of Dalton, Millikan, Rutherford, Moseley, Thomson and Bohr, count protons/neutrons/electrons from atomic and mass numbers, name the four quantum numbers and the rules for filling orbitals, describe s and p orbital shapes, and calculate relative atomic mass from isotopes.

content.heading: Atomic Structure
paragraphs: Everything you have ever touched — including you — is built from particles too small to see. Those particles come in shapes you already know from daily life: single beads, beads joined in pairs, and beads that have gained or lost a charge. Chemistry starts by naming those three shapes correctly.

content.heading: Atoms, molecules and ions in daily words
paragraphs: An atom is one single bead of an element, like one grain of rice. A molecule is atoms holding hands, like a short string of grains. An ion is an atom that has gained or lost an electron, so it carries a charge.

Protons are positive, neutrons neutral. H and He are atoms; H₂O is a molecule; Na⁺ is an ion. Dalton: indivisible atoms in whole-number ratios. Thomson: electron. Rutherford: tiny nucleus. Moseley: atomic number fixes identity. Millikan: charge e. Bohr: shells.
bullets: Atom: one single bead. Molecule: beads holding hands. Ion: a charged bead.
Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Moseley, Millikan, Bohr: one idea each.
content.takeaway: Atoms are single beads, molecules are joined beads, and ions carry a charge.

check.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the three particles?
options: Na is a molecule, Na+ is an atom and NaCl is an ion
Na is an atom, Na+ is an ion and NaCl is a formula unit of a compound
Na is an ion, Na+ is a molecule and NaCl is an atom
Na, Na+ and NaCl are all molecules
check.why: Na is a single atom, Na+ is that atom minus one electron, and NaCl is a formula unit, not a discrete molecule.

content.heading: Counting the three parts of an atom
paragraphs: Think of the atom as a class of people. The proton count names the element, like a school name tag. That count is the atomic number, Z. Protons plus neutrons is the mass number, A. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, so electrons = Z.

Neutrons are simply what is left: neutrons = A − Z. Chlorine has Z = 17, so 17 protons and normally 17 electrons. Isotopes are family members differing only in neutrons, like ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl. The relative atomic mass is the weighted average: (75 × 35 + 25 × 37) ÷ 100 = 35.5.
bullets: Z = protons = the element’s identity.
Neutrons = A − Z; electrons = Z when neutral.
RAM weights isotopes by abundance, not plain average.
content.takeaway: Z counts protons, A − Z counts neutrons, and abundance sets the average.

check.question: For 37Cl, how many protons and neutrons does one atom contain?
check.why: Chlorine has Z = 17, so protons = 17 and neutrons = 37 − 17 = 20.

content.heading: Shells, addresses and shapes
paragraphs: Electrons live on floors (shells) around the nucleus, in rooms called orbitals. Each electron has an address of four quantum numbers: n names the floor, l the room type, ml the exact room, and ms the spin direction.

Three rules govern filling. Aufbau fills the lowest rooms first, like front seats. Hund spreads electrons singly before pairing, like students taking separate seats. Pauli allows at most two electrons per room, spinning opposite ways.
An s orbital is a round cloud holding 2 electrons; a p subshell has three dumbbells holding 6. Chlorine (Z = 17) arranges as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵ — count them: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 5 = 17.
bullets: Shells are floors; orbitals are rooms; quantum numbers are addresses.
Aufbau: lowest first. Hund: singly first. Pauli: two at most.
s = round cloud (2); p = three dumbbells (6).
content.takeaway: Four quantum numbers address each electron, and three rules govern the filling.

check.question: Which set obeyed the Pauli principle for two electrons?
options: 1s2 with ms = +1/2 and -1/2 in the same orbital
1s3 with three electrons in one orbital
2p6 with all six electrons paired in one orbital
check.why: Pauli allows at most two electrons per orbital, and they must have opposite spins.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Before any electron-configuration answer, write Z first and count your electrons to match it. Most lost marks come from a total that does not equal Z.

content.problem: Chlorine has isotopes Cl-35 (75%) and Cl-37 (25%). Calculate the relative atomic mass of chlorine.

steps.reason: Most atoms are Cl-35 and a quarter are Cl-37
Each mass is weighted by how common it is
Percentages must return to a per-atom average

content.question: Bromine has isotopes Br-79 (50%) and Br-81 (50%). Calculate its relative atomic mass.
hints: Multiply each mass by its percentage

content.heading: Go deeper: Why mass number and atomic number differ
paragraphs: Atomic number Z and mass number A answer different questions. Z asks what element it is — the proton count decides the family. A asks how heavy the atom is — protons plus neutrons. Two atoms can share the same Z and still have different A, which is exactly what isotopes are.

Chlorine shows the pair: ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl both have Z = 17 but differ in neutrons (18 versus 20). Calcium-40 and argon-40 show the reverse: same A = 40, but different Z (20 versus 18), so they are different elements with the same mass.

That is why the periodic table is ordered by Z and not by A. Moseley's X-ray work showed Z fixes identity, and the occasional inversion in mass order (argon before potassium) disappears once Z takes over. Mass decides average weight; proton count decides identity.

A useful habit: read the numbers in order — top number A, bottom number Z in the usual symbol — and ask first what Z says, then what A adds. Most isotope errors come from reading the two numbers as one idea.
bullets: Z = identity; A = weight; they are not the same idea.
Same Z, different A = isotopes; same A, different Z = different elements.
The table is ordered by Z (Moseley), not by mass.
Read Z first, then ask what A adds.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the octet is stable
paragraphs: Atoms behave like small rooms whose outer shell wants eight electrons — the octet. Sodium (2,8,1) has one electron in its outer shell and loses it to become Na⁺ with a full (2,8) shell, which is why sodium reacts so eagerly. Chlorine (2,8,7) gains one electron to reach Cl⁻ (2,8,8), completing its octet.

Helium is the exception that proves the rule: its shell holds only two electrons (1s²), the duet, and it is completely inert. Noble gases are inert because their outer shells are already full, and other atoms become stable by matching that arrangement.

This one idea predicts bonding and ion formation. Elements on the left of the table lose electrons to reach a full shell; elements on the right gain them. Hydrogen and helium are the only elements that stop at two.

The octet also explains why metals are conductive and why some compounds form lattice structures: ions with full shells pack stably. Every later lesson on bonding leans on this idea, so it is worth understanding before moving on.
bullets: Outer shell wants 8 electrons (octet); helium wants 2 (duet).
Na loses 1 to fill its shell; Cl gains 1 to fill its own.
Reached-octet atoms are stable and unreactive.
Bonding predictions start from this rule.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in atomic structure
paragraphs: The commonest trap is swapping the two numbers: writing A as the proton count or Z as the mass. The question 'how many protons in ⁴⁰₂₀Ca?' tests exactly that: 20, from Z, not 40. Always hunt for Z first.

The second trap is the plain average of isotope masses. The RAM of chlorine is not (35 + 37) ÷ 2 = 36; it is abundance-weighted and equals 35.5. Averages in chemistry are weighted by how common each part is.

The third trap is electron-counting for ions. Na⁺ has 10 electrons, not 11, because losing one electron changes only the electron count — Z and A stay put. Cl⁻ has 18 electrons for the same reason in reverse.

The fourth trap is configuration totals. After writing a configuration, add the superscripts and check the sum against Z. A sum that does not match Z means the arrangement is wrong, no matter how neatly it looks.
bullets: Protons come from Z, never from A.
RAM is abundance-weighted, not a plain average.
Ions change electron count only; Z and A stay fixed.
Check configuration totals against Z every time.

lessons.title: Chemical Combination
lessons.objective: State the laws of definite, multiple and reciprocal proportions and conservation of mass, write chemical symbols, formulae and balanced equations, and perform mole-concept calculations (moles from mass, concentration, gas volume) and stoichiometry.

content.heading: Chemical Combination
paragraphs: A trader in Onitsha keeps one scale pan for rice and one for beans, and a customer always gets exactly what the scale says. Chemicals combine the same way: in fixed, weighable proportions. This lesson names the three laws behind those proportions and teaches counting by weighing.

content.heading: Three laws in plain words
paragraphs: Conservation of mass says matter is never created or destroyed, only rearranged. Twelve grams of carbon plus 32 grams of oxygen gives 44 grams of carbon dioxide, because 12 + 32 = 44. Nothing is lost.

The law of definite proportions says a compound always has the same mass ratio of its elements. Water is always 1 g of hydrogen to 8 g of oxygen. If the ratio changed, it would be a different compound.

The law of multiple proportions says that when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one combining with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple ratio. Twelve grams of carbon combines with 16 g of oxygen in CO and 32 g in CO₂ — a ratio of 1:2.
bullets: Mass in = mass out; reactions only rearrange matter.
Every compound has a fixed mass ratio of its elements.
Paired compounds use simple whole-number mass ratios.
content.takeaway: Mass is conserved, ratios are fixed, and paired compounds use simple ratios.

check.question: 12 g of carbon forms CO with 16 g of oxygen and CO₂ with 32 g. Which law do 16 and 32 illustrate?
check.why: For a fixed mass of carbon, the oxygen masses 16 and 32 are in the simple ratio 1:2.

content.heading: Formulae and balanced equations
paragraphs: A formula counts atoms: H₂O means two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Symbols are the shorthand — H for hydrogen, O for oxygen — and the subscript is the count. Writing the formula is writing the recipe.
A balanced equation has equal atoms on both sides, since atoms are only rearranged. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O has C1 H4 O4 on both sides. If counts differ, the equation lies about conservation.
Percentage composition gives the empirical formula: divide each percentage by its Ar, then by the smallest value. A compound of 40% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O gives 3.3, 6.7, 3.3, which reduces to CH₂O.
bullets: A formula counts atoms; subscripts are counts.
Balancing means equal atom counts on both sides.
Percentage composition gives the empirical formula.
content.takeaway: Formulae count atoms, equations must balance, and percentages become formulae.

check.question: A compound is 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen. What is its empirical formula?
check.why: Dividing by Ar (12, 1, 16) gives 3.3, 6.7, 3.3, so the ratio is 1:2:1.

content.heading: The mole: counting by weighing
paragraphs: One mole is a counting unit, like a dozen eggs: 1 mole = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. A mole of any substance has the same particle count, but different particles weigh differently, so a mole of carbon and a mole of water weigh different amounts.
Moles come from mass using moles = mass ÷ Mr. Methane has Mr = 16, so 0.5 mol weighs 8 g. One mole of any gas fills 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p., and concentration is moles ÷ volume.
Stoichiometry applies the equation’s mole ratio to real masses. Calcium carbonate (Mr = 100) gives one mole of CO₂ per mole, so 50 g is 0.5 mol and releases 11.2 dm³ of gas at s.t.p.
bullets: 1 mole = 6.02 × 10²³ particles, like a dozen eggs.
Moles = mass ÷ Mr; gas at s.t.p. = 22.4 dm³ per mole.
Stoichiometry applies the equation’s mole ratio.
content.takeaway: A mole counts particles by weighing, and equations give the ratios.

check.question: What is the mass of 0.5 mol of methane, CH₄ (Mr = 16)?
check.why: Mass = moles × Mr = 0.5 × 16 = 8 g.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Changed one unit? Convert cm³ to dm³ first (divide by 1000). Most mole errors in the hall are unit errors, not concept errors.

content.problem: Calculate the mass of 0.5 mol of methane, CH₄ (Mr = 16).

steps.reason: Mass is what weighs, moles is what counts, Mr links them
Half a mole of a Mr of 16 weighs half of 16 grams
A mole in this service is always 6.02×10²³ particles

content.question: Calculate the volume of 0.25 mol of a gas at s.t.p.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why equations must balance
paragraphs: An equation is a scale pan: atoms on the left must equal atoms on the right, because reactions only rearrange. Unbalanced equations pretend atoms appear or vanish, which breaks conservation of mass. Balancing is therefore counting, not decoration.

The counting order that never fails: balance metals first, then non-metals, then oxygen and hydrogen last. Metals rarely appear more than once per side, while oxygen and hydrogen hide inside several compounds and need final checking.

In CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O the carbon balances at once, hydrogen forces 2H₂O, and oxygen then forces 2O₂. Notice the coefficients: doubling H₂O also doubles its oxygen, which is why oxygen is adjusted last.

A systematic candidate counts each element across the whole arrow, not per compound. Total counts, not written counts, decide balance — that is the habit that prevents a balanced-looking equation from being wrong.
A candidate who counts totals before adjusting coefficients balances every equation on the first attempt. The habit costs seconds and saves whole marks.
The system also explains why fractional coefficients are tidied by multiplying the whole equation through: the atom totals do not change, only the presentation.
bullets: Balancing is counting: atoms are only rearranged.
Order: metals, non-metals, then oxygen and hydrogen.
Count totals across the whole arrow, not inside one compound.

content.heading: Go deeper: Empirical and molecular formulae compared
paragraphs: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molecular formula is the true count in one molecule. Glucose and fructose share the empirical formula CH₂O, but only glucose is written C₆H₁₂O₆. The ratio is the same; the size is not.

The link between them is the molar mass. CH₂O has Mr = 30 and glucose has Mr = 180, so 180 ÷ 30 = 6, meaning the true formula is six empirical units. Comparing Mr values converts one formula into the other without any new experiment.

Finding an empirical formula is the reverse journey: percentage composition gives the atom ratio directly, and a measured Mr then scales the ratio up to the molecular formula. Percentages alone can never give the true formula — they only give the ratio.
The exam trap is to stop at the ratio when a molar mass was given. If Mr appears anywhere in the question, the answer needs scaling. No Mr, no scaling: that is the whole discrimination.
Empirical formulae also predict percentage composition, so a candidate can move in either direction between ratio, percentages and true formula in one set of steps.
bullets: Empirical = simplest ratio; molecular = true count.
Scale ratio by Mr ÷ empirical Mr.
Percentages alone never give the molecular formula.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in mole calculations
paragraphs: The first trap is confusing Mr with relative atomic mass: Mr is for a molecule, Ar for an atom. Water's Mr is 18 (2 × 1 + 16), while oxygen's Ar is 16. Using the wrong one changes every mole count after it.

The second trap is skipping the ratio. Two moles of acid may need only one mole of base; multiplying by the equation's ratio comes before any concentration arithmetic. Which is limiting comes from the smaller mole count after dividing by coefficients.
The third trap is s.t.p. values quoted at the wrong temperature. The 22.4 dm³ molar volume belongs to 273 K and 1 atm; at any other temperature the gas law, not the memorised volume, must be used.

The fourth trap is unit mixing: cm³ against dm³, or grams against kilograms. Moles ÷ volume needs dm³, and examiners plant cm³ figures precisely to catch candidates who skip conversion. Convert first, calculate second — always.
Reading the question twice catches the last trap: state the units beside every number as you write, and the habit will expose mismatches before they mark you down.
bullets: Mr is per molecule; Ar is per atom.
Apply the equation ratio before concentrations.
22.4 dm³ belongs only to 273 K and 1 atm.
Convert cm³ to dm³ before dividing.

lessons.title: Kinetic Theory of Matter and Gas
lessons.objective: Apply kinetic theory to distinguish solids, liquids and gases, explain changes of state and Brownian movement, deduce the gas laws from their statements, use the ideal gas equation PV = nRT and vapour density, and state factors that make real gases deviate from ideal.

content.heading: Kinetic Theory of Matter and Gas
paragraphs: Steam rises off a pot of hot yam water, and smoke drifts across a food stall. Both are invisible particles in motion. This lesson explains how the movement of tiny particles explains solids, liquids, gases and every gas law.

content.heading: Particles in motion make solids, liquids and gases
paragraphs: Everything is made of particles that are always moving. In a solid they vibrate in fixed positions. In a liquid they slide past one another. In a gas they move freely everywhere, which is why a gas fills a room.

Melting is particles gaining enough energy to slip past each other. Boiling is energy high enough that particles escape from everywhere at once. Vapourisation, by contrast, escapes only from the surface, at any temperature.

Freezing locks particles into place, and condensation returns a gas to a liquid as it cools. Brownian movement is the visible proof: tiny smoke particles jiggle because invisible air particles keep bumping them.
bullets: Solids vibrate in place; liquids slide; gases move freely.
Boiling bubbles throughout; vapourisation escapes only from the surface.
Brownian movement shows invisible particles bumping visible ones.
content.takeaway: The speed of particles decides whether matter is solid, liquid or gas.

check.question: A puddle dries on a cool day without ever bubbling. Which change is this?
check.why: Vapourisation is escape from the surface at any temperature; boiling bubbles throughout.

content.heading: Six gas laws in daily words
paragraphs: Boyle’s law says squeezing a gas raises its pressure, like crowding a bus. Charles’s law says a gas grows when heated, because faster particles push harder. Gay-Lussac’s law says pressure rises with temperature in a sealed container.

Avogadro’s law says equal volumes hold equal particle numbers, so one mole of any gas fills 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p. Graham’s law says light gases diffuse faster, by the square root of the mass ratio. Dalton’s law says a mixture’s total pressure is the sum of each gas’s pressure.
Each law names which variable is held constant. Reading that condition is the whole skill of applying them.
bullets: Boyle: squeeze a gas and pressure rises.
Charles: heat a gas and volume rises (in kelvin).
Avogadro: equal volumes, equal numbers. Graham: light is faster. Dalton: pressures add.
content.takeaway: Pressure, volume and temperature trade off in fixed, predictable ways.

check.question: A gas is squeezed to half its volume at constant temperature. What happens to its pressure?
check.why: Boyle's law says P ∝ 1/V, so halving V doubles P at constant temperature.

content.heading: One equation that joins them
paragraphs: The ideal gas equation joins all the laws: PV = nRT. P is pressure, V is volume, n is moles, T is temperature in kelvin, and R is a constant. It reads like a recipe: pressure × volume equals amount × temperature (with R).

One mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 dm³ at 273 K and 1 atm, which is the molar volume. The vapour density of a gas is Mr ÷ 2, so a vapour density of 16 means Mr = 32. That link turns a gas measurement into a mass.

Real gases misbehave at high pressure and low temperature, when particles are squeezed close enough that their size and attractions matter. An ideal gas is the strict rule; a real gas is the rule with exceptions.
bullets: PV = nRT joins pressure, volume, amount and temperature.
One mole fills 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p.; vapour density = Mr ÷ 2.
Real gases deviate at high P and low T.
content.takeaway: PV = nRT turns any two measurements into the rest.

check.question: What volume does 1 mol of an ideal gas occupy at 273 K and 1 atm?
check.why: V = 1 × 0.082 × 273 ÷ 1 ≈ 22.4 dm³, the molar volume at s.t.p.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Convert every temperature to kelvin before any gas calculation. Using Celsius instead of kelvin is the single easiest way to fail a gas item.

content.problem: Calculate the volume occupied by 0.5 mol of an ideal gas at 273 K and 1 atm, using R = 0.082 dm³·atm·K⁻¹·mol⁻¹.

steps.reason: Volume is what is asked, so it goes alone
Half a mole at standard temperature holds half the molar volume
Pressure of 1 atm leaves the volume unchanged

content.question: Calculate the volume of 0.5 mol of an ideal gas at 546 K and 1 atm, using R = 0.082 dm³·atm·K⁻¹·mol⁻¹.
hints: Use V = nRT ÷ P as before
Twice the temperature should double the volume from the worked example

content.heading: Go deeper: Why heating makes particles move faster
paragraphs: Temperature is the average speed of particles. Heating a gas hands energy to its particles, so the average speed rises. That is why Charles's law works: faster particles collide harder and push out to a larger volume.

The same idea explains boiling and vapourisation. At the surface, the fastest particles can escape at any temperature, which is vapourisation. Boiling needs the whole liquid to reach the energy where particles escape from everywhere, including bubbles inside.

It also explains why a gas's pressure climbs in a sealed container: the particles hit the walls harder and more often. Gay-Lussac's law is just Charles's law felt on the container instead of measured as volume.
A candidate who pictures collisions instead of formulas can reconstruct every gas law from this one image: speed makes pushing power, and pushing power is pressure.
A candidate who pictures collisions instead of formulas can rebuild every gas law from this one image: speed makes pushing power, and pushing power is pressure.
The same picture explains why perfume spreads: the fastest molecules escape first and race across the room while slower ones lag behind.
Cooling runs the film backwards, slowing particles until some can no longer escape and must condense.
bullets: Temperature measures average particle speed.
Heating raises speed, so gases expand.
Pressure is the force of particles hitting walls.
Pictures of collisions replace memorised laws.

content.heading: Go deeper: Graham's law worked case for hydrogen and oxygen
paragraphs: Graham's law says the rate of diffusion of a gas follows the inverse square root of its molar mass: rate ∝ 1 ÷ √Mr. Hydrogen (Mr = 2) against oxygen (Mr = 32) gives a rate ratio of √(32 ÷ 2) = √16 = 4, so hydrogen diffuses 4 times faster.

In time terms, if oxygen takes 40 seconds to diffuse the same distance, hydrogen takes 40 ÷ 4 = 10 seconds. The lighter gas always wins the race, which is why ammonia fumes cross a classroom long before heavier vapours even start.
The same ratio governs effusion through a tiny hole. A leaking balloon loses hydrogen fastest, not because hydrogen is 'stronger', but because its light particles move quicker between collisions.
The exam trap is inverting the ratio. To correct it, ask first which gas is lighter; the lighter one must have the faster rate, so its number must come out larger.
bullets: Rate ratio = √(heavier Mr ÷ lighter Mr).
H₂ diffuses 4× faster than O₂ (√16 = 4).
The lighter gas always has the faster rate.
Effusion follows the same mass rule.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in gas calculations
paragraphs: The deadliest trap is temperature units. Charles's law and PV = nRT need kelvin; using Celsius compresses or stretches the answer by a huge factor. At 27 °C the correct temperature is 300 K, not 27, and that single slip re-scales every result by about eleven times.

The second trap is vapour density. Vapour density equals Mr ÷ 2, never Mr itself. A vapour density of 16 means a relative molecular mass of 32, not 16. The factor of two is the examiners' favourite silent divider.

The third trap forgets Boyle's condition. If pressure changes, Boyle's law cannot be applied until the temperature is confirmed constant. The question will always bury the condition in plain words like 'the mixture is kept cool'.

The fourth trap is partial pressure addition in the wrong direction: Dalton's law adds pressures of separate gases sharing one container, it does not share one gas's pressure across gases. Reading 'in the same vessel' is the cue to add.
bullets: Always convert to kelvin (27 °C = 300 K).
Vapour density = Mr ÷ 2, never Mr.
Boyle's law needs constant temperature stated or implied.
Dalton's law adds gases sharing one vessel.

lessons.title: Periodic Table
lessons.objective: Relate atomic number to position on the periodic table, relate properties of groups of elements, explain variation of ionisation energy, ionic radii, electron affinity, electronegativity and conductivities across periods and down groups, and identify the alkali metals, alkaline-earth metals, halogens, noble gases and transition metals.

content.heading: Periodic Table
paragraphs: A shopkeeper arranges goods in rows by type: grains together, oils together, soaps together. The periodic table arranges elements the same way — by their electron pattern — so that elements with similar behaviour stand in the same column. This lesson reads that arrangement and the trends it hides.

content.heading: Rows, columns and families
paragraphs: The table is read by atomic number, the proton count. Each row, a period, fills one electron shell, and each column, a group, holds elements sharing the same number of outer electrons. Sodium (Z = 11) sits in period 3 because its electrons fill shells 1 and 2 and start shell 3.

Columns are families with shared behaviour. Group 1, the alkali metals, lose one electron easily. Group 2, the alkaline-earth metals, lose two. Group 17, the halogens, are non-metals that gain one electron. Group 18, the noble gases, are already full and almost never react.

Between the main blocks sit the transition metals, which form coloured compounds and work as catalysts. Their outer electrons sit in inner shells, so they can form several positive ions instead of just one or two.
bullets: Rows (periods) fill one electron shell each.
Columns (groups) share the number of outer electrons.
Group 1, 2, 17, 18 are alkali, alkaline-earth, halogens and nobles.
Transition metals form variable ions and coloured compounds.
content.takeaway: Same column means same outer electrons, and same outer electrons mean similar behaviour.

check.question: Which statement correctly pairs a family with its group?
check.why: Halogens sit in Group 17; the others are placed in different groups.

content.heading: Which way each property moves
paragraphs: Across a period, protons increase while electrons are added to the same shell, so the pull on each electron grows. Atoms therefore shrink, ionisation energy rises, and electronegativity rises. Sodium is a soft metal and chlorine is a reactive non-metal, and that change runs steadily left to right.

Down a group, new shells are added outside, so atoms grow and the outer electrons are shielded from the nucleus. Ionisation energy and electronegativity fall, while metallic character grows. Fluorine, at the top of the halogens, is the most electronegative element of all.

Conductivity follows the same logic: metals conduct because outer electrons are free, and that freedom grows where atoms hold their electrons loosely. Sodium conducts well; chlorine, a non-metal, does not conduct at all.
bullets: Across a period: radius falls, ionisation energy and electronegativity rise.
Down a group: radius grows, ionisation energy and electronegativity fall.
Metallic character fades across and grows down.
Conductivity follows how loosely electrons are held.
content.takeaway: Across a period the pull grows; down a group new shells shield it.

check.question: Which order correctly arranges Na, Mg and Cl by electronegativity?
check.why: Electronegativity rises across the period, so Na < Mg < Cl.

content.heading: Why the trends happen
paragraphs: The root cause is a contest between nuclear charge and shielding. More protons pull harder, but more electron shells push the pull apart. Across a period, charge wins; down a group, shielding wins. Every trend on the table is that contest playing out.

Ionisation energy is the energy needed to pull an electron away. Across a period it rises because the pull grows; down a group it falls because shells shield the outer electron. The noble gases peak only where their full shells resist any change.

Ionic radius shrinks across a period, because the same electron shell is squeezed tighter. Going down, radius grows because each new shell adds a layer. A candidate who remembers the contest can derive any trend without memorising a table.
bullets: Trends come from nuclear charge versus shielding.
Across: charge wins. Down: shielding wins.
Ionic radius follows the same contest.
content.takeaway: Charge pulls in, shielding pushes out, and the winner sets the trend.

check.question: Why does ionisation energy fall down a group?
options: Protons are fewer down the group
New shells are added, so outer electrons are shielded
Electrons are more numerous and pull harder
Atoms lose their neutrons down the group
check.why: Extra shells shield the nucleus, so outer electrons are held less tightly.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When a trend question names two elements, first ask whether moving across or down. The direction decides everything before any values are compared.

content.problem: Arrange sodium, magnesium and chlorine in order of increasing electronegativity.

steps.reason: All sit in period 3, sodium first, magnesium second, chlorine third
steps.result: Na, Mg, Cl left to right

steps.reason: Electronegativity rises left to right in a period
Sodium is the most metallic, chlorine the most electron-hungry

content.question: Arrange fluorine, chlorine and bromine in order of increasing atomic radius, and say why.
hints: All three are halogens in one group
Count the electron shells in each atom
More shells means a larger atom

content.heading: Go deeper: Why ionisation energy rises across but falls down
paragraphs: Ionisation energy is the toll paid to remove an electron. Across a period, each new proton is added to the same electron shell, so every electron feels a stronger pull. The toll therefore rises steadily from sodium to chlorine.

Down a group, each new element adds a whole shell outside the previous one. The outer electrons are not only farther away but shielded by inner shells, so the pull weakens and the toll falls. Potassium costs less to ionise than lithium for exactly this reason.
The trend pauses at the noble gases, whose full shells make a sudden jump in cost. That saw-tooth shape confirms the rule: shell structure, not mass alone, sets the price of removing an electron.
A candidate who explains the trend with charge-versus-shielding language earns full marks; a candidate who recites 'it increases' without the reason earns only part. The mechanism is the mark.
A candidate who explains the trend with charge-versus-shielding language earns full marks; a candidate who recites ‘it increases’ without the reason earns only part. The mechanism is the mark.
The same contest also sets electronegativity, electron affinity and metallic character, so one explanation carries several items.
bullets: Across a period, charge wins and ionisation energy rises.
Down a group, shielding wins and ionisation energy falls.
Noble gases mark the peaks of the saw-tooth trend.
Reasons earn marks; recitation earns part marks.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why atomic radius falls across but rises down
paragraphs: Atomic radius is the distance from nucleus to outer electron. Across a period, protons increase while the shell stays the same, so the pull per electron grows and the atom shrinks. Sodium is larger than chlorine for this reason alone.

Down a group, a new shell is added each step, so even though protons increase, the outer electrons sit a whole layer farther out. Fluorine is therefore much smaller than bromine, despite having fewer protons.
Ionic radius follows the same contest with a twist: Na⁺ is smaller than the Na atom because it lost a shell, while Cl⁻ is larger than Cl because it gained one. Charge changes the shell count itself.
That twist is why radius questions often ask about ions rather than atoms. A candidate who converts the charge into a shell change before comparing will never be trapped.
Radius values quoted for ions come from crystal measurements, and they follow the shell logic exactly: fewer shells, smaller ion; more shells, larger ion.
bullets: Across a period, atoms shrink as protons are added.
Down a group, atoms grow as shells are added.
Na⁺ shrank a shell; Cl⁻ gained one.
Convert the charge to a shell change first.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in the periodic table
paragraphs: The classic trap reverses the two directions: candidates recall that electronegativity rises across the period and then apply that rise down the group, where it actually falls. Before answering, the candidate must name the direction — across or down — and only then choose the rising or falling trend.

The second trap is metallic character. It fades across the period (left is metallic, right is non-metallic) and grows down the group (heavier members are more metallic). Both statements are true; confusing which direction the question asks about is the error.

The third trap is position versus properties. A candidate may state that Group 1 elements 'are reactive' without explaining that each has one outer electron to lose. The charge-versus-shielding mechanism is what earns the full mark.
The fourth trap is reading 'increase' as 'decrease' on a downward question. Writing the two arrows — across ↑, down ↓ — beside every trend question removes this error almost entirely.
bullets: Name the direction before choosing the trend.
Metallic character fades across, grows down.
Reasons (charge vs shielding) earn the full mark.
Write the arrows beside every trend item.

lessons.title: Chemical Bonding
lessons.objective: Distinguish electrovalent (ionic), covalent, coordinate, hydrogen, metallic bonds and van der Waals forces, deduce bond types from electron configurations, relate bonding to properties of compounds, and differentiate the shapes of simple molecules (linear, non-linear, tetrahedral, pyramidal).

content.heading: Chemical Bonding
paragraphs: A mango seller ties a bunch with a short string: sharing. Another counts out coins and hands them over: giving. Atoms do the same two things with electrons — sharing them or giving them — and everything about compounds comes from choosing between those two acts.

content.heading: Giving and sharing electrons
paragraphs: Electrovalent (ionic) bonding is giving: a metal loses electrons and a non-metal gains them, so both become ions that attract each other. Sodium (2,8,1) gives one electron and chlorine (2,8,7) gains one, forming NaCl. The result is a lattice, like a criss-cross of opposite charges.

Covalent bonding is sharing: non-metals share electrons so each reaches a full outer shell. Two hydrogen atoms share their electrons to form H₂, and oxygen shares two pairs to form O₂. Water (H₂O) and methane (CH₄) are covalent because all their atoms are non-metals.

Ionic compounds melt high and conduct when molten or dissolved, because their ions are free to move. Covalent compounds usually melt low and never conduct, because they have no ions to move. Properties therefore announce the bonding.
bullets: Ionic = giving electrons (metal + non-metal).
Covalent = sharing electrons (non-metal + non-metal).
Ionic: high melting, conducts molten. Covalent: low melting, no conduction.
Properties announce the bonding.
content.takeaway: Giving makes ions and crystals; sharing makes molecules; properties tell which.

check.question: Magnesium (2,8,2) and chlorine (2,8,7) react. Which bonding results, and how many of each ion form?
options: Ionic bonding, one Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻
Ionic bonding, one Mg⁺ and one Cl⁻
check.why: Magnesium loses two electrons to become Mg²⁺, and two chlorines each gain one to become Cl⁻.

content.heading: The special bonds
paragraphs: Metallic bonding is giving without keeping: metal atoms drop their outer electrons into a shared sea, and the sea holds the positive cores together. That shared sea is why metals conduct electricity and bend instead of breaking.

Hydrogen bonding is an extra attraction between molecules, not a bond inside one. Water molecules hydrogen-bond to each other, which is why water boils so high compared with similar small molecules. A coordinate (dative) bond is sharing where both electrons come from one atom, as in [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ and [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺.

Van der Waals forces are the weakest attractions between molecules, like the faint stickiness of loose pages. They matter only when stronger bonds are absent, which is why they are mentioned as a special weak force.
bullets: Metallic = shared electron sea; explains conductivity and malleability.
Hydrogen bond = extra attraction between molecules (water, HF, NH₃).
Coordinate bond = sharing where one atom supplies both electrons.
Van der Waals = weakest force between molecules.
content.takeaway: Metallic seas, hydrogen attractions and dative sharing are the special cases.

check.question: In [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺, where do the bonding electron pairs come from?
options: One comes from Cu and one from NH₃
Both come from the NH₃ molecules
Both come from the copper ion
They are free electrons shared by the sea
check.why: In a coordinate bond one atom supplies both electrons — here NH₃ supplies each pair.

content.heading: Shapes of molecules
paragraphs: The shape of a molecule depends on how its atoms arrange around the centre. A linear molecule is a straight line, like CO₂, HCl, H₂, O₂ and Cl₂. A bent (non-linear) molecule folds at the centre, like H₂O, which is why its shape is V-shaped.

A tetrahedral molecule spreads four atoms to the corners of a pyramid, like CH₄. A trigonal pyramidal molecule spreads three atoms with a lone pair at the apex, like NH₃. The lone pair pushes the three atoms down, giving the pyramid its shape.

Shape predicts properties: bent water is polar while linear CO₂ is not, and tetrahedral methane is symmetrical and non-polar. A candidate who can picture the shape can predict polarity without memorising it.
bullets: Linear: CO₂, HCl, H₂, O₂, Cl₂ (straight line).
Bent: H₂O (folds at oxygen).
Tetrahedral: CH₄ (four corners). Pyramidal: NH₃ (apex up).
Shape predicts polarity.
content.takeaway: Counting the arrangement around the centre names the shape.

check.question: Which molecule has a tetrahedral shape?
check.why: Methane spreads its four hydrogen atoms to the corners of a tetrahedron.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Decide bonding from the electron counts first: a metal losing electrons means ionic, two non-metals sharing means covalent. The count decides before the name does.

content.problem: Deduce the bonding in MgCl₂ from the electron counts Mg (2,8,2) and Cl (2,8,7).

steps.reason: Magnesium has 2 outer electrons; chlorine needs 1 to fill its shell
A metal always gives; its 2 electrons go to two chlorines
One Mg²⁺ balances two Cl⁻, and ionic solids melt high

content.question: Sodium (2,8,1) reacts with chlorine (2,8,7). Deduce the bonding, the ions formed and the formula.
hints: Sodium is a metal — what does it do with its one electron?
Chlorine needs one electron — so one sodium feeds one chlorine
Write the ions, then drop the charges into the formula

content.heading: Go deeper: Why ionic compounds conduct only when molten or dissolved
paragraphs: In solid NaCl, the ions are locked in a rigid lattice and cannot move, so no current flows even though charges are present. Melting or dissolving frees the ions to drift to the electrodes, and conduction begins. Conductivity is therefore about freedom of ions, not the mere presence of charge.

Covalent compounds never conduct, even molten, because they contain no ions at all — only neutral molecules. Diamond and graphite differ here because graphite has free electrons between its layers, a rare covalent exception.

A candidate can be tested on the prediction, not the definition: given a new compound's melting point and conductivity, name its bonding. High melting plus conduction when molten means ionic; low melting with no conduction means covalent.
That prediction skill is exactly what JAMB questions measure. Bonding names, shapes and properties are one chain, and the chain starts at the electron count.
The same logic runs backwards: when a solution is evaporated, the ions lock back into a lattice and conduction stops. Freedom of ions is switched on and off by state, not by composition.
JAMB items exploit this directly, asking why solid NaCl fails to conduct while its melt succeeds. The answer is always the locked ions, never the absence of charge.
bullets: Solid ionic: ions locked, no conduction.
Molten or dissolved: ions free, conduction starts.
Covalent: no ions at all, so no conduction ever.
Predict bonding from melting point and conductivity.

content.heading: Go deeper: Hydrogen bonding versus ordinary dipole forces
paragraphs: Ordinary dipole attraction happens between any polar molecules: the positive end of one is faintly attracted to the negative end of another. Hydrogen bonding is a stronger, special case that needs a hydrogen atom bonded directly to N, O or F.

That is why water (H₂O) boils at 100 °C while methane (CH₄), of similar size, boils far lower. Each water molecule hydrogen-bonds to its neighbours, and much heat is needed to break those links. HF and NH₃ show the same elevation.

Van der Waals forces are weaker still and act between all molecules, polar or not. They become noticeable only when hydrogen bonding is absent, which is why small non-polar molecules are gases at room temperature.

The exam ordering — hydrogen bond strongest, then dipole, then van der Waals weakest — is therefore a ranking of separation distances. Stronger attraction means higher boiling point, and the ranking sorts every comparison question.
bullets: Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to N, O or F.
Water boils high because of hydrogen bonding.
Dipole forces are weaker; van der Waals weakest.
Stronger attraction means higher boiling point.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in bonding
paragraphs: The classic trap swaps giving and sharing: candidates call NaCl covalent because 'atoms are joined'. The test is the participants — a metal plus a non-metal always gives, so the bond is ionic. Name the participants first, then the bond.

The second trap is calling any attraction a hydrogen bond. Hydrogen bonding needs H attached to N, O or F; the attraction in HCl is a dipole force, not a hydrogen bond. The bonded atom matters, not the presence of hydrogen alone.

The third trap is the shape swap between NH₃ (pyramidal) and CH₄ (tetrahedral). Counting the atoms is not enough — NH₃ has a lone pair pushing down, which makes it a pyramid with an apex, not a tetrahedron.

The fourth trap is the coordinate bond. It looks like ordinary sharing, but one atom supplies both electrons. In [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ the silver ion accepts pairs from ammonia; the donor is always the ligand, never the metal.
A final trap is calling metal atoms ‘molecules’. Metals are lattices of atoms, not discrete molecules, which is why metals melt as a whole rather than boiling into single atoms.
bullets: Metal + non-metal = ionic, always.
Hydrogen bond needs H on N, O or F.
NH₃ is pyramidal (lone pair); CH₄ is tetrahedral.
In coordinate bonds the ligand donates both electrons.

lessons.title: Separation of Mixtures
lessons.objective: Distinguish elements, compounds and mixtures, differentiate chemical from physical changes, distinguish pure from impure substances, use melting/boiling points as purity criteria, and specify the principle and everyday use of each separation method (evaporation, distillation, sublimation, re-crystallisation, chromatography, crystallisation, magnetisation, decantation, filtration, centrifugation).

content.heading: Separation of Mixtures
paragraphs: A market woman sells mixed goods — stones in beans, husks in rice — and picks them apart by hand. Separating a chemical mixture is the same job with better tools: every method picks components apart using one difference between them.

content.heading: Elements, compounds and mixtures
paragraphs: An element is a substance made of one kind of atom, like oxygen or iron. A compound is two or more elements joined by chemical bonding, like water or carbon dioxide. A mixture is two or more substances merely mixed, like sand and salt in a bowl.

A chemical change makes a new substance with new properties — burning wood gives ash and smoke. A physical change changes only appearance, like melting ice. Mixtures change physically, so their parts can be separated again.

A pure substance melts and boils at exact temperatures; an impure one melts over a range. A sharp melting point therefore proves purity, while a falling melting point reveals impurities. That is why melting and boiling points are purity tests.
bullets: Element = one kind of atom; compound = bonded elements; mixture = mixed substances.
Chemical change makes new substances; physical change does not.
Pure substances melt sharply; impure ones melt over a range.
content.takeaway: Mixtures separate physically because their parts were never chemically joined.

check.question: Which statement correctly pairs a pure substance with its test?
options: A pure substance melts at one exact temperature
Impure substances boil at one exact temperature
check.why: Purity shows as a sharp melting point; impurities spread the range.

content.heading: Separating by heat and air
paragraphs: Evaporation removes a liquid by heating, leaving the dissolved solid: salt from seawater is won this way. Simple distillation separates liquids with different boiling points, like ethanol and water, by boiling and condensing the vapour. Fractional distillation repeats that for many fractions, as in crude oil refining.

Sublimation turns a solid directly into vapour, as with camphor or ammonium chloride, which then deposits back. Re-crystallisation dissolves the solid hot and cools the solution so pure crystals form. Each method exploits one property: volatility, boiling point or solubility.

Magnetisation removes iron with a magnet, as in scrapyards. Decantation pours the liquid off a solid, filtration traps the solid, and centrifugation spins a mixture so the denser part settles outward, as in blood tests.
bullets: Evaporation leaves the salt; distillation separates by boiling point.
Sublimation: solid → vapour → solid (camphor, NH₄Cl).
Magnet removes iron; decantation pours; filtration traps; centrifugation spins.
Every method exploits one property difference.
content.takeaway: Find the property that differs, and that property is the separating tool.

check.question: To obtain pure water from seawater that also contains suspended sand, which order of methods works?
check.why: Filtration removes sand first, then distillation separates water from dissolved salt.

content.heading: Chromatography and crystallisation
paragraphs: Chromatography separates dyes and inks that travel at different speeds along a strip. Paper chromatography dips ink in water; the colours spread out as bands. Column chromatography does the same through a packed tube that holds back some substances longer.

Simple crystallisation grows crystals from a saturated solution by cooling or evaporation. Re-crystallisation purifies: dissolve the impure solid hot, filter while hot, then cool so only pure crystals form while impurities stay dissolved.
In each case the principle is solubility: components dissolve or travel at different rates. A method is chosen by asking which property differs most between the components.
bullets: Paper chromatography separates ink dyes by travel speed.
Column chromatography holds components back differently.
Crystallisation uses solubility; re-crystallisation purifies.
Choose the method whose property differs most.
content.takeaway: Chromatography separates by speed; crystallisation separates by solubility.

check.question: Black ink is mainly one dye that travels as a single band. What does that tell about its composition?
options: It contains several dyes travelling together
check.why: An ink of several dyes would spread into several bands; a single band suggests one travel rate.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Before naming a method, name the property that differs: boiling point, solubility, density or magnetism. The property chooses the method every time.

content.problem: A mixture holds sand, salt and water. Describe a separation that gives pure water.

steps.reason: Sand is insoluble; filter paper traps it while salt water passes
steps.result: Sand is removed as a solid

steps.reason: Water boils and condenses; salt does not distil
steps.result: Pure water is collected, salt remains in the flask

steps.reason: Evaporating to dryness would leave salt mixed with nothing pure to collect
steps.result: Distillation is needed to collect the water itself

content.question: A mixture holds iron filings, sand and water. Give a two-step separation that recovers the iron and the water.
hints: One component answers to a magnet
After that, separate solid from water by filtering
Then distil to collect the water pure

content.heading: Go deeper: Why fractional distillation beats simple
paragraphs: Simple distillation separates two liquids with widely different boiling points. Crude oil holds many fractions with boiling points close together, so one round of boiling cannot divide them. Fractional distillation uses a fractionating column where vapours rise, cool and condense at their own levels.

Each level of the column is a separate still in miniature: vapour condenses, re-boils and rises again. The lightest fraction escapes at the top, while heavier ones leave lower down. The column therefore multiplies the separation without multiplying the apparatus.
The same principle refines air into oxygen and nitrogen, and petroleum into petrol, kerosene and diesel. Whenever boiling points crowd together, fractionation is the answer.
A candidate who links the column to repeated simple distillations will never call a single flask a fractionating column again.

A simple still can split two liquids when their boiling points differ by a wide margin, because the lower-boiling vapour leaves alone. As the gap narrows, contamination rises, and only the column’s repeated boil–condense cycles keep the fractions apart.
bullets: Crude oil fractions boil too close for one still.
The column repeats boil–condense at each level.
Light fractions exit top; heavy fractions exit lower.
Fractionation is repeated simple distillation in one tower.

content.heading: Go deeper: Chromatography as identity evidence
paragraphs: The retention factor, Rf, measures how far a spot travelled relative to the solvent: Rf = distance of spot ÷ distance of solvent. A spot that always travels to the same Rf is the same substance in different hands, which makes chromatography an identity test, not only a separation tool.

Two dyes with different Rf values separate into different bands, and the pattern of bands is a fingerprint. Food colours, inks and plant pigments are all identified this way in food and forensic laboratories.

Paper chromatography depends on solubility and attraction to paper; column chromatography adds adsorption on the packing. Both exploit the same difference: how strongly each component holds on versus travels on.
The exam trap is to treat Rf as a separation product. Rf identifies; it does not manufacture. Discovery of a new spot means a new dye, not a new element.

Because each substance has a fixed Rf under given conditions, matching Rf values in two samples is strong evidence they contain the same dye. Courts and food laboratories rely on exactly this reasoning.
The solvent must be chosen so spots travel a measurable distance without running off the paper. A solvent in which the dye is insoluble gives no evidence at all.
bullets: Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent distance.
Rf patterns identify dyes and pigments.
Paper uses solubility; column adds adsorption.
Rf identifies; it does not create new substances.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in separation
paragraphs: The first trap is melting-point reading. A substance melting over a range is impure, but a substance melting sharply is not necessarily pure — some mixtures melt sharply by coincidence. Sharpness is evidence, not proof, and candidates should state it that way.

The second trap confuses sublimation with evaporation. Evaporation turns a liquid into vapour; sublimation turns a solid directly into vapour. Camphor and ammonium chloride sublime; water evaporates. The starting state decides the name.

The third trap mixes decantation with filtration. Decantation pours the liquid off; filtration passes the mixture through a barrier. If the solid is fine enough to pass the filter, decantation fails and centrifugation is the answer.

The fourth trap is choosing distillation for immiscible liquids. Oil and water separate by decantation long before boiling is needed; distillation is the tool when boiling points differ, not whenever two liquids mix.

A final trap is over-heating during evaporation to dryness, which decomposes some salts. Gentle heating and crystallisation on cooling are the safe route, and the question usually hints at it by asking for crystals.
bullets: Sharp melting is evidence, not proof, of purity.
Sublimation starts from a solid; evaporation from a liquid.
Decantation pours; filtration traps; centrifugation spins.
Immiscible liquids separate without boiling.

lessons.title: Solubility
lessons.objective: Distinguish unsaturated, saturated and supersaturated solutions, interpret solubility curves, calculate the amount of solute that dissolves at a given temperature, relate solvents to their uses, and differentiate true solutions from suspensions and colloids with examples.

content.heading: Solubility
paragraphs: A spoon of sugar disappears into tea while grits stay at the bottom. The sugar dissolved; the grits did not. Solubility is simply how much of a substance a given amount of liquid can dissolve — and this lesson explains the limits.

content.heading: Full, not full, and over-full
paragraphs: An unsaturated solution can still dissolve more, like a half-filled cup. A saturated solution is full: at that temperature it can dissolve no more, and any extra solid settles. A supersaturated solution is over-full — it holds more than the limit because it was cooled carefully without anything to start crystallisation.

A solubility curve shows how much dissolves at each temperature. Most salts dissolve more as water warms, so their curve climbs. Gases behave oppositely: oxygen dissolves less in warm water, which is why warm water holds less dissolved air for fish.

Solubility is written in mol/dm³: moles of solute per cubic decimetre of solution. At saturation, the concentration is fixed by the temperature, not by how much solid you added — extra solid just sits at the bottom.
bullets: Unsaturated: more can dissolve. Saturated: full. Supersaturated: over-full.
Most salts dissolve more when hot; gases dissolve less when hot.
Solubility = moles of solute per dm³ of saturated solution.
content.takeaway: Solubility is a limit set by temperature, and the curve shows how it moves.

check.question: A solution holds more solute than the maximum at that temperature. What is it?
check.why: Holding more than the maximum means the solution is supersaturated.

content.heading: Calculating solubility and choosing solvents
paragraphs: A solubility calculation starts from the definition: how many moles sit in one dm³ of saturated solution. Suppose 11 g of NaCl dissolves in 0.1 dm³. Moles = 11 ÷ 58.5 = 0.188 mol, so the solubility is 0.188 ÷ 0.1 = 1.88 mol/dm³.

Like dissolves like: water, a polar liquid, removes sweat and salt, but not grease. Petrol, an organic solvent, dissolves grease and paint, which is why dry cleaners use it. The solvent is chosen by matching its nature to the stain.

Temperature enters every calculation. A curve reading gives the solubility at the stated temperature, and a supersaturated solution made at a high temperature may crash out crystals as it cools — the basis of re-crystallisation for purification.
bullets: Molar solubility = moles ÷ volume of saturated solution.
Water removes polar stains; petrol removes grease and paint.
The solvent is matched to the nature of the stain.
content.takeaway: Solubility is moles per dm³ at saturation, and the solvent must match the stain.

check.question: Which solvent best removes engine grease from cloth?
check.why: Grease is non-polar like petrol, so petrol dissolves it while water does not.

content.heading: True solutions, suspensions and colloids
paragraphs: A true solution is uniform at the particle level: sugar in water looks clear, passes through filter paper, and never settles. A suspension has particles large enough to see and settle, like muddy water after stirring — Harmattan haze and water paints are suspensions.

A colloid sits between the two: its particles are too small to see or filter but large enough to scatter light. Fog, milk, blood, aerosol sprays, emulsion paints and rubber solution are colloids. The Tyndall effect — a light beam turning visible — is the giveaway.
The particle size decides everything: true solutions pass filter paper; colloids scatter light but do not settle; suspensions settle and are filtered. Size, not appearance, is the distinction.
bullets: True solution: uniform, passes filters, never settles.
Suspension: visible particles, settles, filtered (haze, water paints).
Colloid: invisible particles, scatters light (fog, milk, blood).
Particle size separates the three.
content.takeaway: Size decides: solutions pass, colloids scatter, suspensions settle.

check.question: Which mixture is a colloid?
check.why: Fog scatters light and resists filtration like other colloids, unlike the suspensions and true solution.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Before any solubility number, ask which temperature it belongs to. A solubility quoted without its temperature means nothing, and examiners plant exactly that trap.

content.problem: 11 g of NaCl dissolves in 0.1 dm³ of solution. Calculate its molar solubility.

steps.reason: Moles count particles; Mr(NaCl) = 58.5
Solubility is per cubic decimetre of solution
0.188 × 58.5 = 11.0, so the division is exact

content.question: 23.4 g of NaCl dissolves in 0.2 dm³ of solution. Calculate its molar solubility.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why gases dissolve less when hot
paragraphs: Dissolving a gas means trapping its particles into the liquid. Warming speeds particles up, so they escape more easily — the same reason a hot drink goes flat. Salts behave oppositely because warming helps break their lattice apart.

That opposite behaviour is why solubility curves split into two families: climbing curves for salts, falling curves for gases. Sodium sulfate decahydrate is the exception that proves the rule, falling after about 33 °C when it loses its water of crystallisation.

The practical effect is everywhere: soft drinks are bottled cold to keep gas in, and heating water drives dissolved air out as bubbles. Temperature dependence is not a formula detail; it is visible in every cold drink.
A candidate who explains the escape idea can predict the direction of any curve without memorising it. Hot liquid cannot hold fast-moving gas particles.
The same escape logic explains why heating a soft drink releases bubbles immediately. The gas was only ever loosely held, and warming loosens its grip further.
At the other end, cooling a gas makes it far more soluble, which is why winter lakes hold more dissolved oxygen for fish.
bullets: Gas solubility falls with temperature (particles escape).
Most salts rise; gases fall — two curve families.
Cold drinks stay fizzy because cold holds gas.
One escape picture predicts every direction.

content.heading: Go deeper: Supersaturation and how it forms
paragraphs: A supersaturated solution holds more solute than its temperature allows, but only because crystallisation has not started. Stirring, scratching or adding a tiny crystal starts the process, and the excess falls out until saturation returns.

It is made by dissolving at a high temperature, filtering while hot to remove impurities, then cooling slowly without disturbance. Rock candy is grown exactly this way: a supersaturated sugar solution cooling around a string.
Supersaturation is unstable by definition — the excess wants out. That instability is useful for purification: the excess crashes out as pure crystals while impurities stay dissolved.

The exam trap is calling a supersaturated solution 'concentrated'. Concentration is a measurement; supersaturation is a state beyond the saturation limit. A solution can be concentrated without being supersaturated.
A careful chemist can recrystallise a salt that refuses to dissolve cold: dissolve it hot, remove impurities by hot filtration, then seed the cooling solution with a pure crystal.
Without the seed, a supersaturated solution can sit stable for days — a reminder that stability in chemistry is often only the absence of a beginning.
bullets: Supersaturated = more than the limit, waiting for a start.
Made by hot dissolving, hot filtering, slow cooling.
Used to purify salts by re-crystallisation.
Concentrated is a measure; supersaturated is a state.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in solubility
paragraphs: The first trap confuses solubility with concentration. Solubility is the saturation limit at a temperature; concentration is what is actually present. A dilute solution may be far below its solubility, and a supersaturated one far above.
The second trap mixes gram solubility with molar solubility. Converting between them needs Mr: grams per dm³ divided by Mr gives mol/dm³. Skipping Mr is the commonest calculation error in this topic.
The third trap ignores the curve's temperature. Reading a value from the wrong temperature point is reading a different solution entirely. Always anchor the reading to the stated temperature.
The fourth trap treats colloids as suspensions. Both look milky, but colloids do not settle and pass neither filter nor light beam silently. Particle size, not appearance, decides the class.
A final trap is treating the Tyndall effect as proof of a true solution. Only colloids scatter a beam of light; a clear true solution leaves the beam invisible.
bullets: Solubility is the limit; concentration is the present amount.
Convert g/dm³ to mol/dm³ by dividing by Mr.
Anchor every curve reading to its temperature.
Colloids scatter light; suspensions settle.

lessons.title: Oxidation and Reduction (Redox)
lessons.objective: Classify reactions in terms of oxidation and reduction in their three senses (oxygen, hydrogen/electron transfer, oxidation number), deduce oxidation numbers, balance simple redox equations, compute electrons transferred, name species and agents, and apply oxidation numbers in naming inorganic compounds.

content.heading: Oxidation and Reduction (Redox)
paragraphs: A cut apple browns in the air, and a rusty nail loses its shine. Both are the same kind of change: gaining oxygen or losing electrons. This lesson gives three ways to spot that change and one number that tracks it.

content.heading: Three ways to spot the change
paragraphs: In the oxygen sense, oxidation means gaining oxygen: copper heated in air becomes black copper(II) oxide. Reduction is the reverse — removing oxygen, often with hydrogen: hydrogen strips oxygen from copper(II) oxide and leaves copper metal. The brown apple gains oxygen; the nail gains oxygen.

In the electron sense, oxidation means losing electrons and reduction means gaining them. Sodium becomes Na⁺ by losing one electron, so sodium is oxidised; chlorine becomes Cl⁻ by gaining one, so chlorine is reduced. The memory aid OIL RIG says: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain, of electrons.
In the oxidation-number sense, oxidation is an increase in oxidation number and reduction is a decrease. All three senses describe the same event; they are three languages for one change.
bullets: Oxygen sense: oxidation = gains O; reduction = loses O.
Electron sense: oxidation = loses e⁻; reduction = gains e⁻.
OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain.
Number sense: rise = oxidation, fall = reduction.
content.takeaway: Oxidation and reduction are gain and loss — of oxygen, then of electrons.

check.question: In the reaction 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO, copper is
options: unchanged because oxygen is a spectator
check.why: Copper gains oxygen, and also loses electrons, so it is oxidised.

content.heading: Oxidation numbers as bookkeeping
paragraphs: An oxidation number is a bookkeeping charge assigned to each atom. Free elements are zero; monatomic ions equal their charge; hydrogen is +1 and oxygen is −2; and the numbers sum to zero in a neutral compound.
In H₂SO₄: 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0, so S = +6. In KMnO₄: 1 + Mn + 4(−2) = 0, so Mn = +7. In Cr₂O₇²⁻: 2Cr + 7(−2) = −2, so each Cr = +6.
The change in oxidation number counts electrons moved. Manganese falls from +7 to +2, a fall of 5, so each manganate gains 5 electrons. That count is what balancing uses.
bullets: Free element = 0; monatomic ion = its charge.
H is +1; O is −2; sums to zero in compounds.
Mn in KMnO₄ is +7; S in H₂SO₄ is +6; Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻ is +6.
A fall of 5 in oxidation number means 5 electrons gained.
content.takeaway: Oxidation numbers are bookkeeping: the change counts the electrons.

check.question: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in H₂SO₄?
check.why: 2 + S − 8 = 0 gives S = +6.

content.heading: Balancing, naming and testing
paragraphs: Half-equations balance atoms and charge together. In MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O, manganese falls 5 (from +7 to +2) and iron rises 1 each, so 5 irons match one manganate. Balancing by oxidation number is counting the fall against the rise.
Oxidation numbers name compounds: iron(II) chloride has Fe at +2, iron(III) chloride at +3. The Roman numeral is the oxidation number in words, which is why the same metal gives two different names.

Oxidising agents take electrons: acidified dichromate turns green when reduced. Reducing agents give electrons: hydrogen bleaches hot copper(II) oxide. The agent is named by what it does to the other reactant, not by what happens to itself.
bullets: Balance by matching the oxidation-number change.
Iron(II) = +2; iron(III) = +3 — the numeral names the state.
Oxidising agent takes electrons; reducing agent gives them.
Acidified dichromate turns green when reduced.
content.takeaway: Count the fall against the rise, and the equation balances itself.

check.question: In MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O, which species is the oxidising agent?
check.why: MnO₄⁻ is reduced from +7 to +2, so it oxidises Fe²⁺.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When balancing, write the oxidation-number change under each changing atom first. The matching fall and rise tell you the coefficients before you count charge.

content.problem: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in H₂S₂O₃ (thiosulphuric acid)?

steps.reason: Hydrogen is +1 and oxygen is −2 by the rules
A neutral compound sums to zero
Two sulphurs share the +4 needed

content.question: What is the oxidation number of chromium in Cr₂O₇²⁻?

content.heading: Go deeper: Why oxidation number is bookkeeping
paragraphs: Oxidation number is not a real charge on the atom — it is an accounting entry. In NaCl, sodium has truly lost its electron to chlorine, but in CO the numbers +2 and −2 are formal. The bookkeeping still predicts reactions because it tracks electron movement.
That is why peroxides surprise learners: in H₂O₂ each oxygen is −1, not −2, because they share. The exception only looks like one once the sharing is seen.
Real charge and formal number agree only for ions. For molecules, the number is a tool for balancing, and the tool works precisely because it is consistent.
A candidate who treats the number as a real charge will misjudge covalent compounds. A candidate who treats it as bookkeeping will balance anything.
The bookkeeping is powerful because it is blind to real sharing: it assigns every electron to one atom by fixed rules, so reactions can be balanced without knowing the true electron distribution.
That blindness is also its limit. Oxidation numbers cannot say where electrons truly sit in a molecule, only how they are counted for equation purposes.
bullets: Oxidation number is formal, not a real charge.
Peroxides: O is −1 because of sharing.
The number tracks electron movement for balancing.
Bookkeeping mindset prevents errors in covalent compounds.

content.heading: Go deeper: Balancing half-equations step by step
paragraphs: The MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ case shows the full method. Manganese falls from +7 to +2, a fall of 5, so each manganate gains 5 electrons. Iron rises from +2 to +3, a rise of 1, so one iron gives 1 electron.
Balancing the fall against the rise needs 5 irons per manganate — that fixes the 5 coefficient. Oxygen and hydrogen are then balanced with H⁺ and H₂O, and the charge is checked last.
The charge check is the safety net: left side −1 + 10 + 8 = +17; right side +2 + 15 = +17. Both sides match, so the equation is balanced. A mismatch means an atom count was missed.
The same ladder works for dichromate reductions and any half-equation the syllabus sets. Fall against rise, then atoms, then charge — in that order, every time.
In acid solution the needed H⁺ and H₂O are always available; in alkaline solution OH⁻ and H₂O play that role instead. The medium decides which species appears, and the question will name it.
A candidate who checks charge after every adjustment catches errors at the step where they appear, not at the end of the question.
bullets: Fall of 5 needs 5 irons rising by 1 each.
Balance O and H with water and H⁺, check charge last.
Charge matching is the safety net.
Order: fall vs rise, atoms, charge.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in redox
paragraphs: The classic trap confuses oxidation with the oxidising agent. If copper is oxidised, copper is the reducing agent because it gave the electrons. Naming what a species does to the other reactant is the skill, and the trap reverses it.

The second trap is the sign of the change. A decrease in oxidation number is reduction, even though the atom 'lost' number; students read the smaller number as oxidation. Fall is reduction, rise is oxidation — the number moves opposite to the name.
The third trap is the oxygen rule with peroxides. In H₂O₂ the oxygen is −1, and applying −2 gives a wrong sulphur count in thiosulphates. The shared oxygen is the exception that examiners plant.
The fourth trap is naming. Iron(II) chloride is not iron with two chlorides for fun — the numeral is the oxidation state itself, and swapping II and III swaps the formula.
A final trap is forgetting that an element in a free state is always zero — even nitrogen in N₂ or oxygen in O₂. Assigning it a charge breaks every balance that follows.
bullets: Oxidised species is the reducing agent.
Fall in number = reduction; rise = oxidation.
Peroxide oxygen is −1, not −2.
The Roman numeral is the oxidation state.

lessons.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
lessons.objective: Distinguish the properties of acids and bases, determine basicity, classify normal, acidic, basic and double salts, state methods of preparing salts, relate conductance to degree of dissociation, perform pH and pOH calculations, state the significance of pH, apply buffer solutions, choose indicators, and balance the hydrolysis of salts.

content.heading: Acids, Bases and Salts
paragraphs: A housewife in Onitsha keeps vinegar for stains and caustic soda for blocked drains, and she knows never to mix them. One is an acid; the other is a base. This lesson explains how to tell them apart, what salts are, and how to measure strength.

content.heading: What acids and bases do
paragraphs: An acid is a substance whose water solution gives H₃O⁺ ions — it donates a proton. Acids turn blue litmus red, react with metals and carbonates, and form salts. A base is the opposite: it neutralises an acid, turning red litmus blue and forming a salt.

Basicity counts the hydrogen atoms an acid can donate: HCl is monobasic (one H), H₂SO₄ is dibasic (two H). Strong acids like HCl dissolve fully in water; weak acids like ethanoic acid (vinegar) dissolve only partly. Citric acid in oranges and tartaric acid in tamarind are natural weak acids.

Indicators show the difference without tasting: litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein change colour across the pH range. A buffer solution is a mixture that resists pH change, like the bicarbonate system that holds blood at pH 7.4.
bullets: Acids donate protons; bases accept them.
Strong acids dissociate fully; weak acids partly.
Indicators change colour across the pH range.
Buffers resist pH change.
content.takeaway: Acids donate protons, bases accept them, and indicators show which is which.

check.question: Which definition of an acid follows the proton-donor idea?
options: A substance whose aqueous solution furnishes H₃O⁺ ions
A substance that turns red litmus blue
A substance that neutralises an acid
A substance that conducts electricity only when molten
check.why: Furnishing H₃O⁺ is exactly donating a proton to water.

content.heading: Salts and how they are made
paragraphs: A salt is the neutral product of reacting an acid with a base, metal or carbonate. When all replaceable hydrogen is used, the salt is normal, like NaCl. When some remains it is acidic, like NH₄Cl. When it still carries OH groups it is basic.

A double salt holds two salts crystallised together; alums are the famous example. Salts are prepared by neutralisation (acid + base), by precipitation (two solutions forming an insoluble salt), or by dissolving a metal or carbonate in an acid: Zn + dilute H₂SO₄ gives ZnSO₄ and hydrogen.

How well a solution conducts depends on how far it dissociates. A strong acid dissociates fully and conducts well; a weak acid dissociates partly and conducts weakly. Conductance follows the amount of ions present, not merely the concentration.
bullets: Normal salts use all replaceable H; acidic salts keep some.
Alums are double salts.
Salts: neutralisation, precipitation, or acid on metal.
Conductance follows the ions present.
content.takeaway: Salt type names its leftover hydrogen or hydroxide; strength means dissociation.

check.question: NH₄Cl is an example of which salt type?
check.why: Ammonium chloride carries replaceable hydrogen, so it is an acidic salt.

content.heading: pH, titration and hydrolysis
paragraphs: The pH scale counts hydrogen ions: pH = −log[H⁺]. A solution with [H⁺] = 1×10⁻³ mol/dm³ has pH 3, and pOH = 14 − pH. Pure water sits at 7.

pH matters daily: the stomach works near pH 1–2, soil suits crops near 6–7, and blood holds 7.4. In titration an indicator marks the end point of neutralisation — phenolphthalein for a strong acid with a strong base, methyl orange for a strong acid with a weak base.

Hydrolysis is a salt reacting with water, and it sets the solution’s character. NH₄Cl hydrolyses acidic; Na₂CO₃ hydrolyses basic. Their equations: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺ and CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻. The ion that hydrolyses decides the result.
bullets: pH = −log[H⁺]; pOH = 14 − pH.
Blood 7.4; stomach 1–2; soil 6–7.
Indicator must change near the end point.
NH₄Cl gives acidic; Na₂CO₃ gives basic solutions.
content.takeaway: pH counts hydrogen ions, titration counts moles, and hydrolysis sets the character.

check.question: A solution has [H⁺] = 1×10⁻³ mol/dm³. What is its pH?

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In a titration, find the mole ratio first, then the volumes. The ratio decides everything, so a 1:1 reaction is a straight swap and a 2:1 reaction halves one side.

content.problem: 20.0 cm³ of 0.10 M hydrochloric acid is neutralised by 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide. Find the concentration of the NaOH.

steps.reason: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O is a 1:1 ratio
moles = concentration × volume in dm³ (20.0 cm³ = 0.020 dm³)
0.0020 mol sits in 25.0 cm³ = 0.025 dm³, so C = n/V

content.question: 25.0 cm³ of 0.20 M sulphuric acid is neutralised by an unknown base in a 1:2 ratio (H₂SO₄ : base = 1:2). It takes 40.0 cm³ of the base. Find its concentration.
hints: First find the moles of acid: 0.25 × 0.025
The base has twice as many moles as the acid
Then divide those moles by 0.040 dm³

content.heading: Go deeper: Why conductance follows dissociation
paragraphs: Conductance needs ions to carry charge to the electrodes. A strong acid like HCl dissociates almost completely, so many ions move and conductance is high. A weak acid like ethanoic acid dissociates only partly, so few ions move and conductance stays low at the same concentration.

Dilution makes the contrast sharper: a weak acid dissociates more as it spreads out, so its molar conductance rises on dilution. Strength is about dissociation; concentration is only about amount. A concentrated weak acid can still conduct less than a dilute strong one.
That is the exam link tested: compare two molar solutions, and the stronger acid shows the higher conductance. The degree of dissociation can be read off the conductance ratio directly.
Bases mirror acids: NaOH is strong and conducts well, NH₄OH is weak and conducts poorly although both are bases. Strength, not the acid–base label, sets the ion count.
Comparing a strong and weak acid at the same molar concentration therefore shows a wide conductance gap, and that gap is the practical proof of their different dissociation.
The same measurement ranks bases. The ion count, not the label, always decides.
bullets: Conductance counts the ions actually present.
Strong acids dissociate fully; weak acids partly.
Dilution raises the dissociated fraction of a weak acid.
Strength and concentration are different ideas.

content.heading: Go deeper: Choosing the indicator for a titration
paragraphs: An indicator changes colour across a pH range, so it must change close to the end point of the reaction. Methyl orange changes between pH 3.1 and 4.4, phenolphthalein between 8.2 and 10.0, and litmus changes broadly near 7.
