content.heading: Go deeper: Why water gas is the industrial feedstock
paragraphs: Water gas is made by passing steam over red-hot coke: C + H₂O → CO + H₂. The mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen is called producer gas or water gas, and it is the cheapest large-scale source of hydrogen because coke and water are cheap.

The water-gas shift converts the carbon monoxide further: CO + H₂O → CO₂ + H₂. That step doubles the hydrogen yield per coke and gives a cleaner gas for ammonia synthesis. Industry runs both steps in sequence.
Cracking of petroleum fractions yields hydrogen with alkenes, but the yield per barrel is smaller than the coke route. Scale is why water gas dominates: the feedstock is nearly free.

The exam link is direct: any question asking the industrial source of hydrogen expects water gas (or steam–coke); any question about cracking expects alkenes as the main product, with hydrogen as a by-product.
The shift step is also why syngas is called synthesis gas in industry: the same CO + H₂ mixture feeds ammonia, methanol and oxo processes. One feedstock, several industries.
A candidate who writes both steps — coke to water gas, then shift to hydrogen — shows the full manufacturing chain rather than just the winning name.
bullets: Water gas: steam over coke gives CO + H₂.
Shift: CO + H₂O → CO₂ + H₂ doubles hydrogen.
Cracking yields less hydrogen per barrel.
Industrial source = water gas; cracking = alkenes first.

content.heading: Go deeper: Hydrogen as a reducing agent
paragraphs: Hydrogen removes oxygen from hot metal oxides because it forms water, which is very stable. Copper(II) oxide black turns to copper metal in a stream of hydrogen — a classic laboratory demonstration that reduction is removal of oxygen.
The same power hydrogenates oils in margarine manufacture: nickel catalyses hydrogen adding across double bonds. In ammonia synthesis hydrogen is the reducing partner fed from water gas.

Because hydrogen is the lightest molecule, it diffuses fastest and escapes through the smallest holes. That lightness is why airships abandoned it for helium — flammability plus escape made it impractical at scale.
A candidate who links every use to either lightness or reducing power will never misclassify a hydrogen application.
That same escape tendency is why hydrogen leaks through the smallest joints in stored systems. Engineers must design around the molecule’s size, not ignore it.
In the laboratory the reducing power has a second use: drying and reducing gases before they are dried and tested, where hydrogen removes the last oxygen traces.
bullets: H₂ reduces hot copper(II) oxide to copper.
Hydrogenation and Haber feed on reducing power.
Lightness made airships unsafe; helium replaced it.
Classify uses by lightness or reducing power.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in hydrogen
paragraphs: The classic trap is the preparation. Water gas is the industrial source; metal plus acid is the laboratory one. Questions that name 'red-hot coke' expect water gas, and those naming zinc expect the laboratory method.
The second trap is the pop test. Oxygen rekindles a glowing splint; hydrogen pops with a lighted one. Swapping the two sounds reverses the identification.
The third trap is collectability. Hydrogen is collected by downward air displacement, not over water, because it would diffuse away. The method follows the lightness.
The fourth trap is flammability versus instability. Hydrogen is stable but flammable — it burns cleanly to water. Calling it explosive as a stored gas confuses the burn with the storage hazard.
A final trap is direction: hydrogen reduces copper oxide to copper, but copper never reduces water. The reducer is always the element higher in reactivity, and hydrogen sits mid-series.
bullets: Industrial = water gas; laboratory = metal + acid.
Hydrogen pops; oxygen rekindles — never swap them.
Collected by downward air displacement.
Flammable, but burns cleanly to water.

lessons.title: Chlorine and Hydrogen Chloride
lessons.objective: Predict reagents for the laboratory and industrial preparation of chlorine, identify its properties and uses, determine specific tests for chlorine and chlorides, and predict the reagents for preparation, properties and uses of hydrogen chloride gas and hydrochloric acid.

content.heading: Chlorine and Hydrogen Chloride
paragraphs: The smell of a swimming pool on a hot day is chlorine — the same gas that sterilises the water and bleaches cloth. This lesson follows chlorine from its making to its most important acid.

content.heading: Making chlorine in the laboratory and in industry
paragraphs: The laboratory preparation oxidises hydrochloric acid with manganese(IV) oxide: MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O. The flask is heated gently and the gas is collected by downward displacement of air because chlorine is denser than air.

The industrial preparation electrolyses concentrated brine (saturated NaCl solution): 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂. Chlorine comes off at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode, and sodium hydroxide stays in solution. One cell makes three products.
The choice differs by scale: the laboratory needs a small pure supply, so oxidation wins; industry needs tonnage, so electrolysis of cheap brine wins.
bullets: Laboratory: MnO₂ + conc. HCl, heated gently.
Industry: electrolysis of concentrated brine.
Chlorine is collected by downward air displacement.
content.takeaway: The laboratory oxidises HCl; industry electrolyses brine.

check.question: The industrial preparation of chlorine is by
check.why: Electrolysis of brine is the industrial preparation of chlorine.

content.heading: Properties and uses of chlorine
paragraphs: Chlorine is a greenish-yellow gas with a choking smell, poisonous in quantity. It is a strong oxidising agent: it bleaches damp litmus and removes colour from dyes. That bleaching power is the basis of its uses.
Chlorine sterilises drinking water and swimming pools by killing germs. It bleaches wood pulp for paper and cotton for cloth. It also manufactures hydrochloric acid, plastics (PVC) and insecticides.
The test confirms the gas: chlorine bleaches damp blue litmus paper white. No other common gas does that, so the bleaching is the specific test.
bullets: Greenish-yellow, choking gas; strong oxidising agent.
Uses: water sterilisation, bleaching, HCl, PVC, insecticides.
Test: bleaches damp blue litmus white.
content.takeaway: Chlorine bleaches and kills germs — that is why it is used.

check.question: The specific test for chlorine is that it
check.why: Chlorine's bleaching of damp litmus is its specific test.

content.heading: Hydrogen chloride and hydrochloric acid
paragraphs: Hydrogen chloride gas (HCl) is made in the laboratory by warming concentrated sulfuric acid with sodium chloride: NaCl + conc. H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl. It is collected by downward displacement of air because it is denser than air.

Hydrogen chloride dissolves in water to form hydrochloric acid, a strong acid. The gas and the acid share the name HCl but are different states: the gas is a fuming, pungent compound; the acid is its aqueous solution.

Chlorides are salts of hydrochloric acid. The test for chloride ions (Cl⁻) is silver nitrate solution, which gives a white precipitate of silver chloride, soluble in dilute ammonia. That precipitate confirms the chloride.
bullets: Laboratory HCl: NaCl + conc. H₂SO₄, warmed.
HCl gas dissolves in water to give hydrochloric acid.
Chloride test: AgNO₃ gives a white precipitate.
content.takeaway: HCl gas is made from NaCl and acid; chlorides give a white precipitate with AgNO₃.

check.question: The test for chloride ions is silver nitrate solution, which gives
options: A white precipitate of silver chloride
check.why: Silver chloride is a white precipitate, soluble in dilute ammonia.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For gas preparations, always match the reagents to the scale: MnO₂ + HCl is laboratory, electrolysis of brine is industry. The reagents announce the scale.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why industry electrolyses brine
paragraphs: Brine electrolysis makes three saleable products at once: chlorine at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode, and sodium hydroxide in solution. A plant that buys salt and electricity sells all three, which is why the process dominates chlorine manufacture worldwide.
The laboratory oxidation makes only chlorine, with manganese waste. Electrolysis wins on scale because salt is cheap and the co-products pay for the electricity.
The same cell design explains the Downs process for sodium: remove the water, and sodium itself discharges. One principle — remove the competitor — drives both industries.
A candidate who sees the by-product economics understands why electrolysis, not oxidation, is the industrial answer to any chlorine question.
The diaphragm and membrane cell variants differ only in how they keep the products apart; the chemistry at the electrodes is identical in all three.
Sodium hydroxide is recovered from the catholyte, so the cell is effectively three factories in one vessel. No laboratory oxidation can match that combined output.
bullets: Brine electrolysis sells Cl₂, H₂ and NaOH together.
Laboratory oxidation makes chlorine only.
Remove the water and sodium discharges (Downs process).
By-product economics explains the industrial choice.

content.heading: Go deeper: Chlorine among the halogens
paragraphs: The halogens — fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine — are Group 17 non-metals that gain one electron to form X⁻ ions. Chlorine is the representative because it is the most available and the most studied: greenish-yellow gas, the others being pale yellow, red-brown and purple-black.

Reactivity falls down the group: fluorine is the strongest oxidising agent, iodine the weakest. Displacement reactions show it plainly — chlorine displaces bromine from its salts, bromine displaces iodine, and the reverse never happens.

That order is why chlorine sterilises water efficiently while iodine is used more gently as an antiseptic. Group position predicts behaviour, and the trend is the same charge-versus-shielding contest as the periodic table.
A candidate who recites the displacement order F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ can answer any halogen comparison item without memorising individual reactions.

The displacement order also explains why chlorine water turns starch–potassium iodide paper blue-black in halogen tests: chlorine oxidises iodide to iodine, colouring the paper. The reaction is the test.
A candidate who links displacement to oxidation power answers both the comparison item and the test item from one rule.

That single order of oxidising power also explains electrode positions: fluorine is the strongest oxidising agent of all elements, which is why it is never found free in nature and must be made from its compounds.
bullets: Halogens are Group 17; chlorine is the representative.
Oxidising power falls down the group.
Displacement: Cl₂ displaces Br₂; Br₂ displaces I₂.
Group position predicts behaviour.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in chlorine chemistry
paragraphs: The classic trap is the preparation. Manganese(IV) oxide with concentrated HCl is the laboratory preparation; electrolysis of concentrated brine is the industrial one. Any option naming the other scale loses the mark.
The second trap is the chloride test. Silver nitrate gives a white precipitate with chloride ions; the precipitate is silver chloride, not chlorine gas. The test detects the ion, not the gas.
The third trap confuses HCl gas with hydrochloric acid. The gas is the compound; the acid is its solution. Properties asked about the gas (fuming, dense) do not transfer to the solution unchanged.
The fourth trap is the direction of displacement. Chlorine displaces bromine, never the reverse. Candidates who memorise pairs without direction answer backwards.
A final trap is the state of the chloride test. The white precipitate forms in aqueous solution; dry chlorine gas alone gives no precipitate until it dissolves. Stating the medium prevents the error.
bullets: Laboratory = MnO₂ + HCl; industry = brine electrolysis.
AgNO₃ tests the chloride ion, not chlorine gas.
HCl gas and hydrochloric acid are different states.
Chlorine displaces bromine — never the reverse.

lessons.title: Oxygen, Water and Hardness
lessons.objective: Identify the allotropes of oxygen, determine the significance of ozone, classify the oxides of oxygen and their properties, identify the uses of water, identify the effects of dissolved atmospheric gases in water, distinguish hard from soft water, determine the causes of hardness, identify methods of removing hardness, and describe the treatment of water for town supply, distinguishing water of crystallisation from efflorescence, deliquescence and hygroscopy.

content.heading: Oxygen, Water and Hardness
paragraphs: Every fire needs oxygen, every tap needs water, and every kettle fights the crust that water leaves behind. This lesson follows oxygen from its making, water from its composition, and the hardness that plagues both.

content.heading: Oxygen and its oxides
paragraphs: Oxygen is prepared in the laboratory by heating potassium chlorate with manganese(IV) oxide: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. Industrially it comes from fractional distillation of liquid air. It rekindles a glowing splint, which is its specific test.

Oxygen supports combustion and oxidation; almost every metal and fuel reacts with it, forming oxides. Oxides are classified by their behaviour with acids and bases: acidic oxides (CO₂, SO₂) react with bases, basic oxides (Na₂O, CaO) react with acids, and amphoteric ones (Al₂O₃, ZnO) react with both.

Oxygen has a second allotrope, ozone (O₃), formed when oxygen is exposed to ultraviolet light. Ozone is a pale blue gas with a sharp smell. In the stratosphere it absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation, shielding life on earth.
bullets: Laboratory: KClO₃ + MnO₂, heated. Industry: fractionating liquid air.
Test: rekindles a glowing splint.
Oxides: acidic (CO₂), basic (Na₂O), amphoteric (ZnO), neutral (CO, N₂O).
Ozone (O₃) blocks harmful ultraviolet radiation.
content.takeaway: Oxygen rekindles a splint, and its oxides split into four behaviour families.

check.question: Zinc oxide reacts with both acids and bases. It is
check.why: Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases, like ZnO and Al₂O₃.

content.heading: Water: composition, solvent and dissolved gases
paragraphs: Water is the product of burning hydrogen: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. By volume, two volumes of hydrogen combine with one of oxygen. Every water molecule is H₂O, and its hydrogen bonding makes water the universal solvent — more substances dissolve in it than in any other liquid.

Water dissolves atmospheric gases: oxygen for fish to breathe, carbon(IV) oxide for plants, and nitrogen in small amounts. Those dissolved gases are biologically essential — a pond without dissolved oxygen kills its fish.
Water also dissolves salts, which is why natural waters are never pure. The dissolved load decides the next topic: hardness.
bullets: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O; by volume 2:1.
Water is the universal solvent.
Dissolved O₂ feeds aquatic life; dissolved CO₂ feeds plants.
content.takeaway: Water is H₂O, a universal solvent, and a carrier of dissolved gases.

check.question: Two volumes of hydrogen combine with one volume of oxygen to form water. The volume ratio is
check.why: From 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, hydrogen combines in twice the volume of oxygen.

content.heading: Hard and soft water
paragraphs: Soft water lathers easily with soap; hard water does not, because dissolved calcium and magnesium salts stop the lather and leave scum. Temporary hardness is caused by hydrogencarbonates and is removed by boiling. Permanent hardness is caused by sulfates and survives boiling.

Softening removes the calcium and magnesium: boiling for temporary hardness, adding washing soda for permanent hardness, and ion-exchange resins in modern plants. The salts themselves are not removed from the water's chemistry — they are exchanged or precipitated out.

Water for town supply is treated in stages: screening, coagulation, sedimentation, filtration, chlorination and storage. Each stage removes a different class of impurity, ending with sterile water safe to drink.
bullets: Hardness = Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ salts stop soap lathering.
Temporary (hydrogencarbonates) removed by boiling.
Permanent (sulfates) removed by washing soda or ion exchange.
Town water: screening → coagulation → filtration → chlorination.
content.takeaway: Temporary hardness boils away; permanent hardness needs chemicals or resins.

check.question: Temporary hardness of water is removed by
check.why: Boiling decomposes the hydrogencarbonates that cause temporary hardness.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For water questions, name the dissolved salt first. Hydrogencarbonates mean temporary hardness; sulfates mean permanent — the salt decides the method.

content.problem: Classify water that lathers poorly and whose hardness remains after boiling, and name a softening method.

steps.result: Add washing soda (or use an ion-exchange resin)

content.question: Water lathers poorly but softens on boiling. Classify the hardness and state the cause.
hints: Boiling removes it, so it is temporary
Name the ion pair: calcium and magnesium hydrogencarbonates

content.heading: Go deeper: Water of crystallisation and its three cousins
paragraphs: Crystals grown from water often trap water molecules inside their lattice — water of crystallisation. Blue copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate, CuSO₄·5H₂O, is the classic example: the blue colour is the water, and heating drives it off to leave white anhydrous salt.

Efflorescence is the opposite journey: a hydrated crystal loses its water of crystallisation to the air and turns powdery. Sodium sulfate decahydrate does this on standing. Deliquescence is the reverse of efflorescence — a salt absorbs so much water it dissolves in the absorbed water, like calcium chloride.
Hygroscopy is absorbing moisture without dissolving: silica gel soaks water vapour but stays a solid. Deliquescence dissolves; hygroscopy merely dampens. That boundary is the exam distinction.
The three phenomena are one scale of water affinity: efflorescence loses water, hygroscopy gains it slowly, deliquescence gains it until dissolved. Naming the direction is naming the phenomenon.

Heating a hydrated crystal therefore removes water of crystallisation and changes its colour in the classic blue-to-white copper sulfate test. The colour change is the visible proof that water was part of the crystal.
A candidate who links colour to water content can identify events in a heating curve without any further information.
bullets: Water of crystallisation is trapped in the crystal (CuSO₄·5H₂O).
Efflorescence loses water to air; deliquescence dissolves in gained water.
Hygroscopy absorbs moisture without dissolving (silica gel).
Direction decides the name.

content.heading: Go deeper: Softening and town water treatment
paragraphs: Washing soda (Na₂CO₃) softens permanent hardness by precipitating the calcium and magnesium sulfates as insoluble carbonates. The water trades its hardness salts for soluble sodium salts, which do not interfere with soap.
Ion exchange goes further: resins swap Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ for Na⁺ or H⁺ ions, removing the hardness without adding anything else. The resin is regenerated with concentrated brine when exhausted.

Town supply treatment is a sequence, not a single step: screening removes leaves and debris, coagulation and sedimentation settle fine particles, filtration removes the rest, and chlorination kills germs. Each stage removes a different class of impurity.
Chlorination is last because chlorine would be consumed by the dirt it would otherwise have to kill. Order in treatment is chemistry: first the bulk, then the germs.

That order also explains why chlorination comes after filtration: filtered water needs far less chlorine, so the dose stays low and the taste stays acceptable. Treatment order is economics as well as chemistry.
The same sequence, without the chemical stages, is how rain becomes river water and then groundwater — nature runs the same plants at catchment scale.
bullets: Washing soda precipitates Ca/Mg sulfates as carbonates.
Resins exchange hardness ions for sodium.
Treatment order: screening → settling → filtration → chlorination.
Chlorine works last because dirt would consume it.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in water chemistry
paragraphs: The classic trap is the hardness label. Temporary hardness comes from hydrogencarbonates and boils away; permanent hardness comes from sulfates and does not. The salt names the method, and any option reversing them is false.

The second trap confuses efflorescence with deliquescence. Efflorescence loses water and turns powdery; deliquescence gains water until it dissolves. The direction of water movement is the discrimination, and the exam tests exactly that.
The third trap treats ozone as a pollutant. Stratospheric ozone is protective; ground-level ozone is a pollutant. The layer decides the role, just as with the ozone hole item.

The fourth trap is the volume ratio of water formation. Two volumes of hydrogen combine with one volume of oxygen — candidates who write 1:1 lose the item. From the equation, 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, the volumes follow directly.
bullets: Hydrogencarbonates = temporary; sulfates = permanent.
Efflorescence loses water; deliquescence dissolves in it.
Stratospheric ozone protects; ground ozone pollutes.
H₂:O₂ volume ratio in water is 2:1.

lessons.title: Sulphur and Sulphur Acids
lessons.objective: Identify the allotropes of sulphur and their uses, predict reagents for preparation, properties and uses of SO₂ and H₂S and of H₂SO₄ and H₂SO₃, and determine specific tests for S²⁻, SO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻ and HS⁻.

content.heading: Sulphur and Sulphur Acids
paragraphs: The smell of rotten eggs and the yellow crusts around hot springs are both sulphur. This lesson follows sulphur from its allotropes to the acid that built modern industry.

content.heading: Sulphur and its allotropes
paragraphs: Sulphur occurs as a yellow solid that melts easily and burns with a blue flame to sulfur(IV) oxide. Its allotropes are different arrangements of the same atoms: rhombic sulfur is the common stable form, while plastic sulfur forms when molten sulfur is poured into water and stays soft.

Sulphur is used in vulcanising rubber (mixing it in to harden and strengthen tyre rubber), in matches, in gunpowder and in fungicides. Allotropy — same element, different arrangements — is why one element has several forms with different properties.
Sulphur is a non-metal: it does not conduct electricity and forms acidic oxides. Its chemistry centres on two gases and two acids, each with a preparation, properties and test.
bullets: Sulphur: yellow solid, burns blue; uses in vulcanisation, matches, fungicides.
Allotropes: rhombic (stable) and plastic (soft) sulfur.
Sulphur is a non-metal forming acidic oxides.
content.takeaway: Sulphur's allotropes share the atoms but not the properties.

check.question: Vulcanising rubber means
options: Mixing sulphur into rubber to harden it
Freezing rubber with a cold pack
check.why: Sulphur cross-links rubber chains, hardening and strengthening them.

content.heading: Sulfur(IV) oxide and hydrogen sulfide
paragraphs: Sulfur(IV) oxide (SO₂) is made by burning sulphur in air or roasting sulfide ores. It is a colourless acidic gas that dissolves in water to give sulfurous acid, H₂SO₃, and reacts with alkalis to give trioxosulfate(IV) salts.

Hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) is made from iron(II) sulfide and dilute hydrochloric acid: FeS + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂S. It smells of rotten eggs. As a weak acid it behaves as a reducing agent, and as a precipitating agent it forms insoluble metal sulfides.

The tests separate them: SO₂ turns acidified dichromate green and bleaches coloured solutions, while H₂S turns lead(II) acetate paper black (PbS). The rotten-egg smell itself is a warning sign, not the test.
bullets: SO₂: from burning S or roasting ores; acidic oxide; bleaches; dichromate turns green.
H₂S: FeS + dilute HCl; rotten-egg smell; weak acid and reducer.
H₂S turns lead acetate paper black (PbS).
content.takeaway: SO₂ is the bleaching acid gas; H₂S is the rotten-egg reducer.

check.question: Hydrogen sulfide turns lead(II) acetate paper
check.why: Lead(II) sulfide (PbS) is black, confirming H₂S.

content.heading: Trioxosulfate(IV) and tetraoxosulfate(VI) acids
paragraphs: Trioxosulfate(IV) acid (H₂SO₃) is formed when SO₂ dissolves in water, and its salts are the trioxosulfate(IV) salts. Acids turn those salts back into SO₂, which is their distinguishing reaction: effervescence of a choking gas that bleaches.

Tetraoxosulfate(VI) acid (H₂SO₄) is made industrially by the Contact process: SO₂ is oxidised to SO₃ over V₂O₅, then absorbed to give the acid. It is the king of acids — dilute it behaves as a strong dibasic acid, concentrated it oxidises and dehydrates.

The tests separate the sulfur anions: SO₃²⁻ gives SO₂ with acids, SO₄²⁻ gives a white precipitate with BaCl₂ (barium sulfate, insoluble in acid), and S²⁻ gives black PbS with lead acetate. Each anion has one reliable witness.
bullets: H₂SO₃ forms from SO₂ + water; acids liberate SO₂ from its salts.
H₂SO₄ by Contact process; concentrated = oxidising and dehydrating.
SO₃²⁻ → SO₂ with acid; SO₄²⁻ → white BaSO₄; S²⁻ → black PbS.
content.takeaway: Sulphur's acids and salts each carry one unmistakable test.

check.question: The test for sulfate ions (SO₄²⁻) is
options: Acids give a choking gas that bleaches
BaCl₂ gives a white precipitate insoluble in dilute acid
check.why: Barium sulfate is a white precipitate insoluble in dilute acid — the sulfate test.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For every sulfur anion question, write its witness first — SO₂ gas, white BaSO₄, or black PbS. The witness is the answer, and everything else is decoration.

BaSO₄ is insoluble in dilute acid, unlike sulfite or carbonate precipitates

content.heading: Go deeper: Why concentrated sulfuric acid is two reagents
paragraphs: Dilute sulfuric acid is simply a strong dibasic acid: it donates two protons and behaves like any strong acid. Concentrated acid is a different reagent entirely — it oxidises carbon to carbon dioxide and dehydrates sugars to black carbon.

The oxidising power comes from the sulfate ion itself: hot concentrated acid oxidises copper to copper(II) sulfate while being reduced to SO₂. Dilute acid cannot do this; concentration changes the reagent's nature.
Dehydration is the removal of water's elements: sugar with concentrated acid chars to carbon, and ethanol dehydrates to ethene. The acid takes H₂O out of the substrate rather than adding to it.
A candidate who separates the two personalities — dilute acid versus concentrated oxidiser/dehydrator — will never misclassify a reaction of the acid.
The dehydrating power is why concentrated acid is stored away from organic materials: it will char paper, wood and sugar on contact, extracting water and leaving carbon behind.
That charring is also a test: concentrated acid blackens sugar instantly, while dilute acid does nothing of the kind. The reagent difference is visible in one drop.
bullets: Dilute H₂SO₄ = strong dibasic acid only.
Concentrated = oxidising (Cu → CuSO₄ + SO₂) and dehydrating (sugar → C).
Concentration changes the reagent's nature.
Two personalities, two reaction families.

content.heading: Go deeper: The Contact process as applied equilibrium
paragraphs: The Contact process oxidises SO₂ to SO₃: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, exothermic with fewer molecules forward. Moderate temperature, high pressure and a V₂O₅ catalyst maximise the equilibrium yield — the same Le Chatelier logic as the Haber process.
The SO₃ is then absorbed not directly in water (which would make a mist) but in concentrated sulfuric acid, forming oleum. Diluting oleum gives the acid without the mist problem.

Sulfuric acid is the largest-volume chemical made anywhere, and its production is a fair measure of a nation's industrial strength. The process is therefore both an equilibrium exercise and an industrial landmark.
A candidate who connects the Contact process to equilibrium has learned two topics in one: the chemistry of sulfur and the economics of Le Chatelier.

The catalyst V₂O₅ does not shift the equilibrium; it only reaches it faster. The yield is set by temperature and pressure, exactly as Le Chatelier predicts for an exothermic, molecule-reducing reaction.
A candidate who reads the Contact process as equilibrium with a catalyst has answered both the sulfur item and the equilibrium item at once.
bullets: Contact: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, exothermic, fewer molecules.
Moderate T, high P, V₂O₅ catalyst.
Absorbed via oleum to avoid mist.
Sulfuric acid output measures industrial strength.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in sulfur chemistry
paragraphs: The classic trap is the oxidation states. In SO₂ sulfur is +4, in SO₃ and H₂SO₄ it is +6, and in H₂S it is −2. Writing the state beside every formula removes most sulfur errors.

The second trap confuses bleaching with the test. SO₂ bleaches as a reducing agent (it removes oxygen); chlorine bleaches as an oxidising agent. The decolourisation looks identical — the mechanism is opposite.

The third trap is the precipitate's acid solubility. Sulfate's BaSO₄ is insoluble in dilute acid; sulfite's precipitate dissolves with effervescence. Forgetting the acid step collapses the two tests into one.
The fourth trap is allotrope versus compound. Rhombic and plastic sulfur are elements; SO₂ is a compound. Preparation questions about allotropes are never expected — only their existence and uses.
A final trap is the sulfur oxidation ceiling. Sulfur(VI) in sulfuric acid is the highest common state; any calculation giving sulfur more than +6 has an arithmetic error, not a new compound.
bullets: S in SO₂ is +4; in SO₃/H₂SO₄ +6; in H₂S −2.
SO₂ bleaches by reducing; Cl₂ by oxidising.
BaSO₄ is acid-insoluble; sulfite precipitate dissolves.
Allotropes are elements; preparation is not expected.

lessons.title: Ammonia and Nitrogen Compounds
lessons.objective: Specify the laboratory and industrial preparation of NH₃, identify its properties and uses, determine specific tests for NH₄⁺ and NH₃, identify reagents for the laboratory preparation of HNO₃ with its properties and uses, and specify the properties of N₂O, NO and NO₂ with their specific tests.

content.heading: Ammonia and Nitrogen Compounds
paragraphs: The sharp cleaning smell from a bottle of household ammonia is a nitrogen compound — the same gas that feeds the world's farms. This lesson follows ammonia from its making to the acid it becomes.

content.heading: Making ammonia
paragraphs: The laboratory preparation warms an ammonium salt with a strong base: NH₄Cl + NaOH → NH₃ + NaCl + H₂O. The gas is dried over quicklime (CaO) and collected by downward displacement of air, because it is lighter than air and very soluble in water.

The industrial preparation is the Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, at about 450 °C, 200 atm, over an iron catalyst. Nitrogen comes from fractional distillation of liquid air, hydrogen from water gas. High pressure favours the fewer-molecule side.
Ammonia is collected over concentrated sulfuric acid in the laboratory when dryness is not needed — it forms white fumes of ammonium salts with hydrogen chloride as the classic confirmation.
bullets: Laboratory: ammonium salt + strong base, warmed.
Industry: Haber process (450 °C, 200 atm, iron catalyst).
Collected by downward air displacement; dried over CaO.
content.takeaway: The laboratory warms an ammonium salt; industry balances nitrogen and hydrogen.

check.question: The laboratory preparation of ammonia uses
check.why: Warming an ammonium salt with a strong base liberates ammonia in the laboratory.

content.heading: Properties and uses of ammonia
paragraphs: Ammonia is a colourless gas with a sharp smell, very soluble in water to form an alkaline solution (ammonium hydroxide). It is a base: it neutralises acids to form ammonium salts. With hydrogen chloride it gives dense white fumes — the classic test.
Ammonia is a reducing agent: it reduces hot copper(II) oxide to copper. It also forms complex ions with metal ions, like [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺, which is why it appears in qualitative analysis.

Its uses follow from those properties: ammonium sulfate and urea fertilisers feed crops, refrigeration uses its easy liquefaction, and household cleaners use its alkalinity. The test for ammonia gas is white fumes with hydrogen chloride; the test for NH₄⁺ is warming with a base and the same fumes.
bullets: Very soluble in water; alkaline solution; forms white fumes with HCl.
Reducing agent; forms complex ions.
Uses: fertilisers, refrigeration, cleaners.
Test: NH₃ + HCl → dense white fumes.
content.takeaway: Ammonia is a soluble alkaline gas that fumes white with HCl.

check.question: The specific test for ammonia gas is
options: It forms dense white fumes with hydrogen chloride
check.why: Ammonia and hydrogen chloride form white ammonium chloride fumes.

content.heading: Trioxonitrate(V) acid and its salts
paragraphs: Trioxonitrate(V) acid (HNO₃) is prepared in the laboratory from ammonia: ammonia is oxidised catalytically to nitrogen(IV) oxide, then to nitrogen dioxide, which dissolves in water to give the acid. It is a strong, oxidising acid.
HNO₃ is used in fertilisers, explosives and the pickling of metals. Its salts are the trioxonitrate(V) salts (nitrates), which decompose on heating to nitrites and oxygen: 2NaNO₃ → 2NaNO₂ + O₂.

The test for nitrate ions (NO₃⁻) is brown fumes of NO₂ when heated with concentrated sulfuric acid. The oxides of nitrogen — N₂O, NO and NO₂ — complete the family: colourless N₂O (laughing gas), colourless NO, and brown NO₂.
bullets: HNO₃ from ammonia oxidation; strong oxidising acid.
Nitrates decompose on heating to nitrites + O₂.
Nitrate test: brown NO₂ fumes with conc. H₂SO₄.
Oxides: N₂O colourless, NO colourless, NO₂ brown.
content.takeaway: Nitric acid is made by oxidising ammonia; nitrates give brown fumes.

check.question: The test for nitrate ions is
options: Brown fumes of NO₂ with concentrated sulfuric acid
A squeaky pop with a lighted splint
check.why: Heating nitrates with concentrated sulfuric acid liberates brown nitrogen dioxide.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For nitrogen questions, track the oxidation state: NH₃ is −3, NO is +2, NO₂ is +4, HNO₃ is +5. The state names the compound before its uses do.

One mole of N₂ gives two moles of NH₃

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the Haber process needs a compromise
paragraphs: The Haber reaction is exothermic, so cooling favours ammonia — but at low temperatures the reaction is too slow to matter. The plant runs at about 450 °C because that is where speed and yield compromise. Iron catalyst speeds the approach without shifting the position.

High pressure favours the fewer-molecule side (4 gas molecules become 2), so 200 atm pushes the yield up. Higher pressure would push further but costs more to build and run. Unreacted gases are recycled, so low per-pass yield is recovered over many passes.
The same logic runs the Contact process: moderate temperature, high pressure, V₂O₅ catalyst. Two industries, one principle — Le Chatelier managed by engineers.
A candidate who sees the Haber conditions as a compromise, not a maximum, answers every 'why these conditions' item correctly.
The recycle loop is itself an application of Le Chatelier: unreacted gases are returned so the forward reaction consumes them again, recovering over many passes what a single pass leaves behind.
A candidate who sees the loop will recognise recycling as equilibrium management, not waste handling.
bullets: 450 °C: compromise between yield (cold) and rate (hot).
200 atm: favours 2 NH₃ over 4 gas molecules.
Recycling recovers unreacted gases over many passes.
Same logic as Contact: Le Chatelier plus economics.

content.heading: Go deeper: Ammonia as a ligand and a test
paragraphs: Ammonia's lone pair makes it a ligand: it donates both electrons of a coordinate bond to metal ions, forming complex ions like [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺. That is why excess ammonia dissolves copper(II) hydroxide to a deep blue solution — a qualitative-analysis landmark.
The same lone pair makes ammonia a base: it accepts a proton to form NH₄⁺. The acid–base and ligand roles are one property — the available electron pair — used in two different reactions.
The white-fume test exploits both: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl solid fumes. The reaction is instant and unmistakable, which is why it confirms ammonia beyond doubt.
A candidate who links the lone pair to both behaviours will never memorise them as separate facts.
bullets: NH₃ lone pair donates into coordinate bonds.
Excess NH₃ dissolves Cu(OH)₂ to deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺.
NH₃ + HCl → white fumes: the specific test.
One lone pair explains base, ligand and test.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in nitrogen chemistry
paragraphs: The classic trap is the preparation. Warming an ammonium salt with a base is the laboratory preparation; the Haber process is the industrial one. Any option naming the other scale loses the mark.

The second trap is the oxidation state of nitrogen. In NH₃ it is −3, in NO +2, in NO₂ +4, and in HNO₃ +5. Nitric acid is not 'the acid with nitrogen at +5' by memory — the state follows from the sum rule, and candidates should compute it.
The third trap is the fume test direction. Ammonia fumes with hydrogen chloride (white); chlorine bleaches litmus. Swapping the two tests reverses the identification.

The fourth trap is nitrates versus nitrites. Heating a nitrate gives a nitrite plus oxygen; the test for nitrate is brown NO₂ fumes with concentrated sulfuric acid. The two reactions are related but not interchangeable.
A final trap is the state of the ammonia solution. Ammonium hydroxide is a weak base in equilibrium with NH₃ gas; warming it drives off ammonia, which is why the laboratory preparation works at all.
The same equilibrium explains why ammonia bottles are labelled with the pressure of the gas: the solution is a stored gas waiting to escape.
bullets: Laboratory = ammonium salt + base; industry = Haber.
N states: NH₃ −3, NO +2, NO₂ +4, HNO₃ +5.
White fumes = ammonia test; bleaching = chlorine test.
Nitrate test gives brown NO₂ fumes.

lessons.title: Carbon and Its Oxides
lessons.objective: Identify the allotropes of carbon, predict reagents for the laboratory preparation of CO₂, specify its properties and uses, determine reagents for the laboratory preparation of CO, predict the effects of CO on humans, determine specific tests for HCO₃⁻, CO₃²⁻ and CO, identify the different forms of coal, determine their uses, specify products of the destructive distillation of wood and coal, and specify the uses of coke and synthesis gas.

content.heading: Carbon and Its Oxides
paragraphs: Pencil lead, diamonds and charcoal are all the same element: carbon. This lesson follows carbon through its forms, its two oxides, and the fuels dug from the ground.

content.heading: Allotropes of carbon
paragraphs: Allotropy means one element, different arrangements. Carbon has three famous forms. Diamond is the hardest natural substance, each atom bonded to four others in a rigid network — that is why it cuts glass and glitters in jewellery.

Graphite is soft and slippery: its atoms form layers that slide over each other. The layered structure makes it a lubricant and the 'lead' in pencils. Amorphous carbon is the shapeless form found in charcoal and coke, used as an adsorbent.
Other allotropes include fullerenes (buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀) and nanotubes, used in advanced materials. The properties follow the arrangement: hard diamond, slippery graphite, porous charcoal.
bullets: Diamond: hardest; rigid network; cuts glass.
Graphite: layered, soft; lubricant and pencil 'lead'.
Amorphous carbon: charcoal, coke; adsorbent.
Fullerenes (C₆₀) and nanotubes are advanced forms.
content.takeaway: Same atoms, different arrangements: hard diamond, soft graphite, porous charcoal.

check.question: Graphite is used as a lubricant because
options: It is the hardest natural substance
Its layers slide over each other
It is a good electrical non-conductor
It melts at a low temperature
check.why: Graphite's layered structure lets the layers slide, making it slippery.

content.heading: Carbon(IV) oxide and carbon(II) oxide
paragraphs: Carbon(IV) oxide (CO₂) is made in the laboratory from calcium carbonate: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O. It is a colourless, dense gas, fire-extinguishing (it smothers flames by blanketing), and slightly soluble in water to form carbonic acid.
The test for CO₂ is limewater turning milky: CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O. Carbonates and hydrogencarbonates also give CO₂ with acids, so the test confirms the gas, not the salt.

Carbon(II) oxide (CO) is made by passing steam over red-hot coke: C + H₂O → CO + H₂. It is a colourless, odourless, poisonous gas, reducing hot metal oxides. It binds haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen — that is why charcoal fires kill in closed rooms.
bullets: CO₂: CaCO₃ + acid; test = limewater milky; extinguishes fire.
CO: steam over coke; poisonous; binds haemoglobin.
Sources of CO: charcoal, fires, exhaust fumes.
content.takeaway: CO₂ milks limewater and smothers fire; CO is odourless poison.

check.question: The specific test for carbon(IV) oxide is
check.why: CO₂ forms insoluble white CaCO₃ with limewater, making it milky.

content.heading: Coal, coke and synthesis gas
paragraphs: Coal is graded by carbon content: peat is youngest, then lignite, bituminous coal, and anthracite (hardest, richest in carbon). The older the coal, the more carbon and the more heat it gives.

Destructive distillation heats coal or wood without air: coal gives coke, coal gas, ammonia liquor and coal tar; wood gives wood gas, acetic acid and methanol. Coke is the solid left behind, used as a fuel and reducing agent in metallurgy.
Coke gasified with steam and air makes synthesis gas (syngas): a mixture of CO and H₂ used to make methanol, ammonia and synthetic fuels. Producer gas is the leaner version used directly as a fuel.
bullets: Coal grades: peat < lignite < bituminous < anthracite.
Destructive distillation: coke + gas + tar + ammonia liquor.
Coke gasification makes synthesis gas (CO + H₂).
content.takeaway: Older coal is richer in carbon; distillation and gasification unlock its products.

check.question: Coke is obtained by
check.why: Coke is the solid residue left when coal is heated in the absence of air.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For carbon questions, first ask which oxide: CO is poisonous and reducing, CO₂ is acidic and milky-limewater. The oxidation state decides the story.

content.problem: Calcium carbonate reacts with excess dilute HCl to give CO₂. Calculate the volume of CO₂ at s.t.p. from 10 g of CaCO₃. (CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O; Mr CaCO₃ = 100)

steps.reason: Mr(CaCO₃) = 100, so grams convert by dividing by 100
One mole of carbonate gives one mole of CO₂
One mole of gas fills 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p.

content.question: 20 g of calcium carbonate reacts with excess dilute acid. Calculate the CO₂ volume at s.t.p. (Mr = 100).

content.heading: Go deeper: Why diamond is hard and graphite is soft
paragraphs: Diamond's hardness is structural: every carbon is bonded to four others in a three-dimensional network, so there is no direction in which layers can slide. The hardness is the network itself.
Graphite's softness is the opposite structure: strong sheets with only weak forces between them. The sheets slide, so graphite cleaves into flakes and coats surfaces as a lubricant.

The same structures explain conductivity: diamond has no free electrons and is an insulator, while graphite's free electrons between layers conduct electricity. Structure decides property, and the exam tests exactly that link.
A candidate who pictures the network versus the layers can predict hardness and conductivity for any carbon form without memorising either.
The same layer picture explains why diamond cleaves along planes and why graphite writes: each application exploits the weak inter-layer forces rather than the strong bonds within layers.
Fullerenes extend the idea into curved sheets: C₆₀ closes graphite-like layers into a ball, which is why it behaves between the two classic forms.
bullets: Diamond: 3D network — hard, insulating.
Graphite: sliding sheets — soft, conducting.
Structure decides property; the exam tests the link.
Picture network vs layers to predict behaviour.

content.heading: Go deeper: Carbon monoxide as a poison
paragraphs: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin about 200–300 times more strongly than oxygen does. Once bound, the haemoglobin cannot carry oxygen, so the blood's oxygen delivery collapses even though the air contains oxygen.

That is why charcoal fires and faulty generators kill in closed rooms: the CO is colourless and odourless, the victim notices nothing, and the blood is quietly taken over. The danger is silent because the gas gives no smell and no irritation.
CO is also a reducing agent: it removes oxygen from hot copper(II) oxide. The same property that makes it a poison makes it a useful reducer in metallurgy.
The exam trap is to treat CO as merely 'a greenhouse gas'. Its primary danger is haemoglobin binding, not the greenhouse effect.
Treatment is removal from the source and fresh air, because the binding is reversible only slowly. Prevention — ventilation and complete combustion — is the real control.
That reversibility is also why CO poisoning is survivable: given oxygen and time, the haemoglobin releases CO and reloads with oxygen.
bullets: CO binds haemoglobin 200–300× stronger than O₂.
No smell, no irritation — silent poison.
CO reduces hot metal oxides (metallurgy).
Primary danger is blood binding, not greenhouse effect.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in carbon chemistry
paragraphs: The classic trap is the limewater test. Limewater turns milky with CO₂ — but if excess CO₂ is passed, the milkiness disappears as soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate forms. The test must be stopped at the first milkiness.
The second trap is oxidation state. In CO₂ carbon is +4; in CO it is +2. Writing the state beside every formula prevents calculating the wrong number of electrons.
The third trap is anthracite versus coke. Anthracite is the richest natural coal; coke is a manufactured residue. One is dug, the other is distilled, and the question will name which.
The fourth trap is carbon(II) oxide's sources. Charcoal, fires and exhaust fumes all produce CO by incomplete combustion; complete combustion gives CO₂. The oxygen supply decides the oxide.

A final trap is the water-gas shift. Passing CO with steam gives CO₂ and more hydrogen, which is how industry maximises hydrogen from coke: C + H₂O first, then CO + H₂O. The two steps are one process, not two products.
bullets: Excess CO₂ clears limewater milkiness — stop at first white.
C in CO₂ is +4; in CO is +2.
Anthracite is dug; coke is manufactured.
Incomplete combustion → CO; complete → CO₂.

lessons.title: Metal Properties and Extraction
lessons.objective: Specify the general properties of metals, determine the method of extraction suitable for each metal, relate the methods of extraction to the properties of the metals, and compare the chemical reactivities of the metals.

content.heading: Metal Properties and Extraction
paragraphs: A nail, a wire and a cooking pot are all metal, and all of them conduct, shine and bend. Those shared habits come from one structure — a sea of electrons — and that same structure decides how each metal is dug out of the ground.

content.heading: The shared habits of metals
paragraphs: Metals share habits because they share a structure: positive metal cores in a sea of free electrons (metallic bonding). The free electrons conduct electricity and heat, reflect light, and let atoms slide past each other, which is why metals are malleable and ductile.

Most metals are hard, dense and high-melting, but the exceptions are memorable: sodium is soft enough to cut with a knife, mercury is liquid at room temperature, and lead is soft and dense. Properties follow electron looseness: the looser the sea, the softer the metal.

Chemically, metals lose electrons to form positive ions. Their reactivity follows position: potassium and sodium react fiercely with water, zinc and iron react with acids, and gold and platinum barely react at all.
bullets: Metallic bonding: free electron sea in a lattice of cations.
Conductivity, shine, malleability and ductility all come from the sea.
Reactivity = how readily a metal loses electrons.
content.takeaway: One electron sea explains the shared habits and the reactivity order.

check.question: Metals conduct electricity because
options: They contain free electrons moving through the lattice
check.why: The free electron sea carries charge through the metal.

content.heading: The reactivity series and extraction
paragraphs: The reactivity series ranks metals by how eagerly they lose electrons: K, Ca, Na, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au. Hydrogen sits in the middle as the reference. A metal higher up displaces a lower one from its compounds.

Extraction follows the series. Reactive metals (K, Na, Al) are won only by electrolysis, because no cheaper reagent can pull their electrons away. Middle metals (Zn, Fe) are won by carbon reduction in a blast furnace. Unreactive metals (Ag, Au) are found free or by simple leaching.
The rule is economic as much as chemical: the higher the metal, the more expensive its extraction. That is why aluminium was once precious and gold was always found as nuggets.
bullets: Series: K, Ca, Na, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au.
Higher metal displaces a lower one from solution.
Top metals: electrolysis. Middle: carbon reduction. Bottom: found free.
content.takeaway: The series predicts both reactivity and the extraction method.

check.question: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis because
options: It is too reactive for carbon reduction
It melts at a low temperature
check.why: Aluminium sits above zinc in the series, so carbon cannot displace it from its oxide.

content.heading: Displacement and corrosion
paragraphs: Displacement is the series in action: zinc dipped in copper(II) sulfate solution coats itself with copper while zinc ions enter solution. Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Iron displaces copper the same way, which is why iron nails can be copper-plated without electricity.
Corrosion is the reverse journey: iron rusts because it loses electrons to oxygen and water. It is an electrochemical process, and it happens fastest where air and water meet the metal together.

Protection follows the series: paint and grease block air and water; galvanising coats iron with zinc, which corrodes first sacrificially; tin is only a barrier, and once scratched, iron rusts faster.
bullets: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu (displacement).
Rust is iron losing electrons to oxygen and water.
Galvanising protects sacrificially; tin only barriers.
content.takeaway: Higher metals displace lower ones, and corrode before them.

check.question: An iron nail dipped in copper(II) sulfate solution becomes coated with copper because
options: Copper is more reactive than iron
Iron is more reactive than copper and displaces it
check.why: Iron sits above copper in the series, so it displaces copper ions.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For any displacement or extraction item, first write the metals in series order. The higher one always wins the reaction.

content.problem: Zinc is dipped in copper(II) sulfate solution. Write the reaction and state whether it is displacement.

steps.operation: Place zinc and copper in the series
steps.reason: Zinc sits above copper, so zinc is more reactive
steps.result: Zn above Cu: displacement will happen

steps.reason: Zinc gives electrons, copper ions gain them
The ions combine with the sulfate spectator unchanged

content.question: Iron is dipped in zinc sulfate solution. Does any reaction happen? Give a reason from the series.
hints: Find iron and zinc positions in the series
The higher metal displaces the lower — never the reverse
Iron is below zinc, so nothing happens

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the electron sea explains everything
paragraphs: The electron sea is the single idea behind metallic properties: conductivity because electrons move, malleability because atoms slide without breaking bonds, shine because the sea reflects light, and thermal conduction because electrons carry heat fast.

Reactivity is sea looseness measured. Sodium's outer electron is loosely held, so it leaves instantly; gold's electrons are tightly held, so it stays free in nature. The series is a looseness ranking.
That is why extraction costs track the series: pulling a tight electron away needs electrolysis, pulling a loose one needs only carbon. Economics and chemistry are the same ranking read twice.
A candidate who holds the sea picture answers property, reactivity and extraction items from one image instead of three lists.
The same sea explains why alloys are harder than pure metals: foreign atoms break up the sliding planes, so they resist deformation. Steel’s hardness over iron is the sea picture applied.
A candidate who holds the sea picture answers property, reactivity and extraction items from one image instead of three lists.
bullets: Conductivity, shine, malleability: one electron sea.
Reactivity = looseness of the outer electrons.
Extraction cost tracks the same looseness.
One picture answers three item families.

content.heading: Go deeper: Rusting as an electrochemical cell
paragraphs: Rusting needs both oxygen and water: dry iron in oxygen does not rust, and iron in boiled water without air does not rust. The two together make a tiny cell on the iron's surface, with rust forming at the oxygen-rich spots.
That is why the waterline of a ship rusts fastest — oxygen is plentiful there and the metal is wet. The cell model predicts the pattern exactly.

Galvanising works because zinc is the better anode: it oxidises instead of iron. Tin on a scratched can does the opposite — tin is less reactive than iron, so once the coating breaks, the iron becomes the anode and rusts faster.
Painting and greasing are barriers, not sacrifices. They work only while unbroken, which is why scratched paint is worse than no paint at the scratch.

Stainless steel resists rusting differently: its chromium forms a thin, self-healing chromium oxide film that seals the surface. The protection is a barrier that repairs itself, unlike scratched paint.
Galvanised roofing therefore outlasts painted iron in the same rain: one barrier heals by sacrifice, the other fails at the first scratch.
bullets: Rusting needs both oxygen and water.
The waterline rusts fastest — oxygen-rich and wet.
Zinc protects sacrificially; tin only barriers.
Scratched paint is worse than no paint.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in metals
paragraphs: The classic trap is the extraction method. Carbon reduces zinc oxide but not aluminium oxide; any option giving carbon reduction for aluminium or sodium is false. The series decides, not the metal's abundance.
The second trap is displacement direction. Iron displaces copper; copper never displaces iron. Writing the series from memory before answering prevents reversals.
The third trap is hydrogen's position. Metals above hydrogen displace it from dilute acids; metals below do not. Copper with dilute HCl gives no reaction, whatever the acid.
The fourth trap is corrosion protection. Sacrificial protection needs a more reactive metal (zinc); tin on iron only barriers. Once scratched, the tin-coated iron rusts faster than bare iron.

A final trap is the hydrogen line. Metals above hydrogen react with dilute acids to give hydrogen; metals below — copper, silver, gold — do not react at all. The line is the reference, not the acid strength.
bullets: Aluminium needs electrolysis; carbon fails above the line.
Displacement goes one way only: higher displaces lower.
Metals below hydrogen do not react with dilute acids.
Zinc protects sacrificially; scratched tin accelerates rust.

lessons.title: Sodium and Its Compounds
lessons.objective: Determine the method of production of sodium hydroxide by electrolysis of brine and its action on aluminium, zinc and lead ions, determine the production of sodium trioxocarbonate(IV) and sodium hydrogen trioxocarbonate(IV) by the Solvay process with their properties and uses, determine the occurrence of sodium chloride in sea water and its uses and economic importance with the test for Na⁺.

content.heading: Sodium and Its Compounds
paragraphs: Salt from sea water, soda for glass, and caustic soda for soap all reach back to one soft metal that catches fire in water. This lesson follows sodium from the sea to its three great compounds.

content.heading: Sodium hydroxide from brine
paragraphs: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH, caustic soda) is produced by electrolysing concentrated brine (saturated NaCl solution): 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂. The three products are hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode, and NaOH in solution — one cell, three sales.

NaOH is a strong base that precipitates metallic hydroxides from their salts: 2NaOH + Al³⁺ → 2Na⁺ + Al(OH)₃, and the same with Zn²⁺ and Pb²⁺. Those precipitates are the qualitative-analysis tests for those ions.
Its uses follow its strength: soap and detergent manufacture, paper pulping, aluminium extraction, and the neutralisation of acidic gases. Caustic soda is the workhorse alkali of industry.
bullets: Brine electrolysis: H₂ cathode, Cl₂ anode, NaOH solution.
NaOH precipitates Al³⁺, Zn²⁺, Pb²⁺ as hydroxides.
Uses: soap, paper, aluminium processing, neutralisation.
content.takeaway: Brine electrolysis makes caustic soda, and caustic soda precipitates metallic hydroxides.

check.question: Sodium hydroxide is produced industrially by
check.why: Electrolysis of brine produces NaOH with H₂ and Cl₂ as co-products.

content.heading: Washing soda and the Solvay process
paragraphs: Sodium trioxocarbonate(IV) (Na₂CO₃, washing soda) is produced by the Solvay process, in which brine is reacted with ammonia and carbon(IV) oxide. The key step forms sodium hydrogen trioxocarbonate(IV) (NaHCO₃), which is heated to give Na₂CO₃.

Na₂CO₃ is used in glass manufacture (it lowers the melting point of sand), in soap, in water softening and in detergents. Sodium hydrogen trioxocarbonate(IV) (NaHCO₃, baking soda) is used in baking, fire extinguishers and as an antacid.
Heating sodium hydrogencarbonate gives the carbonate and water: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O. The carbonate is therefore the 'baked' form of the hydrogencarbonate.
bullets: Solvay process: brine + NH₃ + CO₂ → NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃.
Na₂CO₃: glass, soap, water softening, detergents.
NaHCO₃: baking, extinguishers, antacid.
content.takeaway: Solvay bakes hydrogencarbonate into washing soda for glass and soap.

check.question: Sodium trioxocarbonate(IV) (washing soda) is used in
check.why: Na₂CO₃ lowers the melting point of sand in glass manufacture.

content.heading: Sodium chloride from the sea
paragraphs: Sodium chloride occurs dissolved in sea water and as rock salt. Its recovery is solar evaporation: sea water is pumped into shallow ponds and the sun evaporates it until salt crystallises. The process is cheap because the fuel is sunlight.

Salt is the feedstock of the chlor-alkali industry: electrolysis of brine gives chlorine, hydrogen and NaOH, and from those come plastics, acids and soaps. Salt also preserves food, seasons it, and melts ice on roads.
The test for Na⁺ is the flame colour: sodium gives a persistent golden-yellow flame. That colour is specific enough to confirm the ion in a mixture.
bullets: NaCl occurs in sea water; recovered by solar evaporation.
Salt feeds the chlor-alkali industry (Cl₂, H₂, NaOH).
Na⁺ flame test: persistent golden yellow.
content.takeaway: Sea salt is solar-won and feeds the whole chlor-alkali industry.

check.question: The flame colour of sodium is
check.why: Sodium gives a persistent golden-yellow flame — its specific test.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For sodium questions, trace the feedstock: salt in, and chlorine, hydrogen and caustic soda out. The products name the process.

content.problem: Write the ionic equation for the precipitation of aluminium hydroxide by sodium hydroxide.

steps.reason: Aluminium solution has Al³⁺; NaOH supplies OH⁻
steps.result: Al³⁺ and OH⁻ meet in solution

steps.reason: Three hydroxides balance one aluminium charge
Aluminium hydroxide is a white gelatinous precipitate

content.question: Write the ionic equation for the precipitation of zinc hydroxide by sodium hydroxide.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the Solvay process is clever
paragraphs: The Solvay process is clever because it wastes nothing: the ammonia used in the first step is recovered from the by-products and fed back. The net inputs are brine, limestone and carbon dioxide; the outputs are washing soda and calcium chloride.
The insoluble sodium hydrogencarbonate is the key: it precipitates from the reaction mixture, so it can be filtered and heated cleanly to the carbonate. Solubility differences do the separating.
That is why the process replaced the older Leblanc process, which produced mountains of waste. Process chemistry is often the art of the precipitate: making the product fall out cleanly.
A candidate who sees the recycling and the precipitate understands why Solvay, not Leblanc, is the answer to any washing-soda question.
The calcium chloride by-product is not waste in modern plants: it is sold for de-icing roads and dust control. A well-designed process turns even its remainder into a product.
That completeness is why Solvay remains the world standard a century later. Efficiency, not novelty, keeps it in use.
bullets: Ammonia is recovered and recycled in Solvay.
Insoluble NaHCO₃ precipitates for easy separation.
Solvay replaced Leblanc (waste) with recycling.
Precipitation is the separating trick.

content.heading: Go deeper: The chlor-alkali industry as one cell
paragraphs: Chlor-alkali means chlorine plus alkali from one cell. Electrolysing brine gives chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide together, and each product feeds a different industry: chlorine to plastics and acids, hydrogen to ammonia, caustic soda to soap and paper.
The economics explains the geography: chlor-alkali plants sit near salt and cheap electricity, because those are the two inputs that cannot be moved. Chemistry plants follow their feedstocks.
Sodium metal itself is won from fused NaCl (Downs process), completing the picture: the same salt feeds the metal, the alkali and the gas.
A candidate who traces salt through all three products has learned sodium chemistry as a system, not as three facts.
The same economics explains why caustic soda prices move with electricity prices: power is half the cost of the cell. When power is cheap, alkali is cheap; when power rises, soap and paper follow.
A candidate who links the product prices to the electricity bill understands the industry better than one who memorises the equation.
bullets: One cell, three products: Cl₂, H₂, NaOH.
Plants sit near salt and cheap power.
Salt also feeds sodium metal (Downs process).
Trace salt through every product.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in sodium chemistry
paragraphs: The classic trap is the Solvay product. The process makes washing soda (Na₂CO₃) via the hydrogencarbonate, not caustic soda. Caustic soda comes from brine electrolysis; washing soda comes from Solvay. The two processes are never interchangeable.
The second trap is the flame colour. Sodium is golden yellow, potassium is lilac, calcium is brick red. Swapping flame colours reverses the identification.

The third trap is the precipitate test. Sodium hydroxide precipitates Al³⁺, Zn²⁺ and Pb²⁺ as hydroxides — but the ions are the metals', not sodium's. Na⁺ itself stays in solution and is tested by flame, not by precipitation.
The fourth trap is the direction of the Solvay bake. Heating hydrogencarbonate gives carbonate, never the reverse. Baking drives off CO₂ and water; no amount of heating in air returns them.
A final trap is the evaporation step. Salt won by solar evaporation is crude and needs purification before the cell; sea water cannot go straight into an electrolyser without fouling it.
The ponds are staged by density so that impurities crystallise out before the salt does. Purification is part of the recovery, not an afterthought.
bullets: Solvay = washing soda; brine electrolysis = caustic soda.
Na⁺ flame is golden yellow; K⁺ is lilac.
NaOH precipitates the metal ions, not Na⁺.
Heating NaHCO₃ gives Na₂CO₃ — never backwards.

lessons.title: Calcium and Cement
lessons.objective: Specify the properties and uses of calcium oxide, calcium hydroxide and calcium trioxocarbonate(IV), describe the preparation of calcium oxide from sea shells, specify the chemical composition of cement, describe the setting of mortar, and determine the test for Ca²⁺.

content.heading: Calcium and Cement
paragraphs: Every house in Nigeria stands on calcium — in its walls, its mortar and its cement. This lesson follows the metal from sea shells to building sites.

content.heading: Calcium oxide, hydroxide and carbonate
paragraphs: Calcium oxide (CaO, quicklime) is made by heating limestone or sea shells strongly: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. It is a white solid that reacts violently with water to give calcium hydroxide.
Calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)₂, slaked lime) forms when water is added to quicklime: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂. It is a base used in mortar, whitewash and water treatment. Its solution is limewater.
Calcium trioxocarbonate(IV) (CaCO₃, limestone) is the starting rock: it decomposes on heating, reacts with acids to give CO₂, and forms the basis of cement. The test for Ca²⁺ is a brick-red flame.
bullets: CaO: heated limestone/sea shells (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂).
Ca(OH)₂: slaked lime; used in mortar and water treatment.
CaCO₃: limestone; tested by brick-red flame for Ca²⁺.
content.takeaway: Heating limestone gives quicklime; water slakes it to limewater.

check.question: Calcium oxide is prepared from sea shells by
check.why: Sea shells are calcium carbonate; heating decomposes them to CaO and CO₂.

content.heading: Cement: composition and setting
paragraphs: Cement is a mixture of calcium silicates and aluminates, made by heating limestone with clay to about 1450 °C. The clinker is ground with gypsum to produce cement powder. Its main components are tricalcium silicate, dicalcium silicate and tricalcium aluminate.

Mortar is cement mixed with sand and water. It sets — hardens — by hydration: water reacts with the calcium silicates to form strong gels and calcium hydroxide. Setting is a chemical reaction, not drying.
Concrete is mortar with stones added. All three harden by hydration, and all three gain strength over days as the reaction continues. That is why new concrete is kept wet: curing feeds the reaction.
bullets: Cement: limestone + clay heated to ~1450 °C, ground with gypsum.
Main components: calcium silicates and aluminates.
Setting = hydration of the silicates, not drying.
content.takeaway: Cement sets by hydration; concrete and mortar are the same chemistry with aggregate.

check.question: The setting of mortar is a chemical process in which
options: Water reacts with calcium silicates to form hard gels
Air is trapped in the mixture
check.why: Hydration of calcium silicates forms the hard gel that sets the mortar.

content.heading: Uses of the calcium compounds
paragraphs: Calcium oxide is used in cement, steel-making, and neutralising acidic soils. Calcium hydroxide is used in mortar, whitewash, water softening and the treatment of acidic soils. Calcium carbonate is used in cement, glass, and as a filler.
Limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) is the test for carbon(IV) oxide, turning milky. That same solution neutralises acidic gases and softens water.
The test for Ca²⁺ is a brick-red flame colour. Calcium ions give that colour in a flame test, confirming the ion in any mixture.
Calcium carbonate also neutralises acidic soils in the field and builds reefs in the sea. One compound, three industries.
bullets: CaO: cement, steel-making, soil neutralisation.
Ca(OH)₂: mortar, water treatment; limewater tests CO₂.
Ca²⁺ flame test: brick red.
content.takeaway: The three calcium compounds feed building, soil treatment and tests.

check.question: The flame colour of calcium ions is
check.why: Calcium gives a brick-red flame — its specific test.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For calcium items, follow the chain in order: carbonate heated to oxide, oxide slaked to hydroxide. The preparation names the process each time.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why cement needs gypsum
paragraphs: Gypsum is ground with clinker to make cement, and without it the cement would set almost instantly. Tricalcium aluminate reacts with water too fast, and gypsum slows it by forming a protective layer that controls the pace.
That controlled pace is what building trades need: enough working time to place the mortar, then a predictable hardening. Gypsum is therefore not a filler but a regulator.
The setting time also depends on fineness: finer cement hydrates faster and sets sooner. Grinding is part of the chemistry of speed.
A candidate who links gypsum to aluminate control understands cement manufacture as managed hydration, not just heating.
Without gypsum, the first water on cement would trigger a flash set — the mix would harden in minutes, long before it could be placed. The gypsum layer buys the working time the trade needs.
That window is measured in minutes and hours, and it is the reason cement is ground with gypsum in the mill rather than added on site. Control is built into the powder.
A candidate who names aluminate control as the role of gypsum has explained the only reason it is there. Anything else — strength, colour, cheapness — is decoration.
bullets: Gypsum slows tricalcium aluminate hydration.
Working time is the product; speed is the risk.
Finer cement sets faster; grinding controls speed.
Cement manufacture is managed hydration.

content.heading: Go deeper: Curing concrete
paragraphs: Hydration needs water throughout the hardening period, so new concrete is kept wet — covered or sprayed — for days. Dried-out concrete stops gaining strength because the reaction stops.
That is why curing is specified on building sites: the chemistry continues long after the pour, and strength is built in the second and third weeks, not the first day.
The same logic explains why mortar mixed too dry never reaches strength: the silicates have no water left to react with. Water is a reactant in setting, not just a mixer.
A candidate who treats curing as watering understands that concrete is still reacting weeks after it looks finished.
The strength gain follows the hydration curve: fast in the first days, then slower for weeks. That is why tests are run at 7 and 28 days, not on the day of the pour.
Mass concrete faces the opposite problem: hydration heat builds up inside, so large pours need cooling. The same reaction that strengthens can crack if its heat has nowhere to go.
bullets: Hydration needs water for days — keep concrete wet.
Strength builds in weeks, not on day one.
Water is a reactant, not just a mixer.
Dry concrete stops reacting and stays weak.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in calcium chemistry
paragraphs: The classic trap is the setting mechanism. Mortar sets by hydration (reaction with water), not by drying. Any option describing evaporation or air exposure misnames the process.
The second trap is the flame colour. Calcium is brick red, sodium golden yellow, potassium lilac. Swapping them reverses the identification.
The third trap is the order of the chain. Carbonate heated gives oxide; oxide plus water gives hydroxide. Reversing the order writes an impossible preparation.
The fourth trap is gypsum's role. It is a regulator of setting time, not a main component or a filler. Naming it as the setting agent reverses its function.

A final trap is calling limewater a base only. Limewater is calcium hydroxide solution, and its milky test with CO₂ is a precipitation of CaCO₃. The base and the test reagent are the same solution used two ways.
bullets: Setting = hydration, not drying.
Ca²⁺ flame is brick red.
Carbonate → oxide by heat; oxide + water → hydroxide.
Gypsum regulates setting time.

lessons.title: Aluminium and Tin
lessons.objective: Specify the method of purification of bauxite, the electrolytic extraction of aluminium, the properties and uses of aluminium and its compounds, and determine the test for Al³⁺; specify the ores of tin, relate the method of extraction to its properties, and specify the uses of tin.

content.heading: Aluminium and Tin
paragraphs: A cooking pot that does not rust and a food tin that seals tight are both made from metals pulled out of rock by electricity and fire. This lesson follows aluminium from its ore to its tests, and tin from its ore to its uses.

content.heading: Aluminium: purification and extraction
paragraphs: Bauxite is the ore of aluminium, a reddish rock rich in aluminium oxide. It is purified by the Bayer process: the oxide dissolves in hot concentrated NaOH, impurities are filtered off, and pure aluminium oxide precipitates and is calcined. That pure oxide is called alumina.

Alumina is electrolysed dissolved in cryolite (Na₃AlF₆), which lowers its melting point and saves energy. At the cathode, aluminium ions gain electrons and deposit as metal; at the carbon anode, oxide ions discharge as oxygen, which burns the anode away.

Aluminium sits high in the reactivity series, so carbon cannot reduce it — only electrolysis wins its electrons. Its extraction is therefore electricity-hungry, which is why aluminium is made near cheap power.
bullets: Bayer process purifies bauxite to alumina.
Alumina electrolysed in cryolite; oxygen burns the anode.
Aluminium needs electrolysis because it sits high in the series.
content.takeaway: Bauxite is purified to alumina, and alumina is electrolysed in cryolite.

check.question: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis rather than carbon reduction because
options: It is too reactive for carbon to displace it
It melts at too low a temperature
It does not occur in nature
check.why: Aluminium sits high in the series; carbon cannot pull its electrons away.

content.heading: Properties, uses and the test for Al³⁺
paragraphs: Aluminium is light (density one-third of iron), does not rust because its oxide film seals it, conducts well, and is malleable. Those four properties explain its uses: aircraft bodies, cooking pots, overhead cables and foil.

Its compounds include aluminium oxide (the abrasive itself), aluminium chloride and aluminium sulfate (used in water treatment). The oxide film is amphoteric: it reacts with both acids and bases, which is why aluminium dissolves in both.

The test for Al³⁺ is sodium hydroxide solution, which gives a white gelatinous precipitate of Al(OH)₃ that dissolves in excess NaOH. That double behaviour — precipitate, then dissolve — is specific to aluminium.
bullets: Light, rust-proof (oxide film), conducting, malleable.
Uses: aircraft, pots, cables, foil.
Al³⁺ test: white gelatinous precipitate with NaOH, soluble in excess.
content.takeaway: Aluminium's oxide film makes it light, rust-proof and useful — and Al³⁺ precipitates white with NaOH.

check.question: The test for Al³⁺ with sodium hydroxide solution gives
options: A white gelatinous precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH
check.why: Al(OH)₃ is white and gelatinous, and it dissolves in excess alkali.

content.heading: Tin: ore, extraction and uses
paragraphs: Tin is mined from cassiterite ore (SnO₂). The ore is concentrated by gravity because cassiterite is dense, then reduced with carbon in a furnace: SnO₂ + C → Sn + CO₂. Carbon works because tin sits low in the reactivity series.

Tin is a soft, silvery metal that resists corrosion and is used to coat iron (tin plate for food cans), in alloys like soft solder and bronze, and in some electrical work. Tin plate protects because tin forms a barrier — but as the earlier lesson showed, a scratched coating lets iron rust faster.
Tin's uses follow its properties: low melting point for soldering, corrosion resistance for coating, and softness for alloying. Each use is a property read off the metal.
bullets: Ore: cassiterite (SnO₂); extraction by carbon reduction.
Uses: tin plate, soft solder, bronze, electrical work.
Scratched tin plate accelerates rusting of iron.
content.takeaway: Tin comes from cassiterite by carbon reduction and coats iron against rust.

check.question: Tin is extracted from cassiterite by
check.why: Tin sits low in the series, so carbon displaces it from its oxide.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For extraction questions, locate the metal in the series first. The position names the method — electrolysis, carbon, or found free — every time.

content.problem: Alumina is electrolysed in cryolite. At which electrode does aluminium form, and why not carbon reduction?
